title: Red letters for the sale
text: Big red letters [spells|spell|'Letters' is plural, so use 'spell'.] ‘SALE’ in the shop window. The other words are small and black. People can read the red word from across the road. They know [their|there|'There are' tells us something exists; 'their' means 'belonging to them'.] are lower prices before they see the clothes. A person who wants [an|a|Use 'a' before a consonant sound: a cheap shirt.] cheap shirt may cross the road to look inside.

title: The green arrow to the café
text: [A|An|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an arrow.] arrow on the street [point|points|'An arrow' is singular, so add -s: points.] to the left. Under it, the sign says ‘Tea and cake’. People can read the sign while they walk. They know what they can buy and which way to go. Someone who wants to sit down for a cup of tea can [finds|find|After 'can', use the base verb: find.] the café easily.

title: The number on the lemonade sign
text: ‘£1 a cup’ is the [bigest|biggest|Spelling: double the g in 'biggest'.] line on the sign. The word ‘Lemonade’ [are|is|'The word' is singular, so use 'is'.] just below it. People can see the price before they stop at the table. A child with one pound in their pocket can look at the sign and know they have enough [moneys|money|'Money' is uncountable: no -s.] to buy a drink.

title: A phone case on the floor
text: A phone falls from a table in the advert. We [here|hear|'Hear' is what you do with your ears; 'here' means 'in this place'.] it hit the floor. The woman [pick|picks|'The woman' is singular, so add -s: picks.] it up, and the screen still works. The picture shows what the case can do. People who drop [there|their|'Their' means 'belonging to them'.] phones at home may see a reason to put a case on their own phone.

title: A light for the school bag
text: At the start of the advert, a girl looks in her bag after dark. She cannot find her [keyes|keys|The plural of 'key' is 'keys'.]. Then she [turn|turns|'She' takes -s: she turns.] on a little light in the bag and finds them. We see the problem and the answer. A student with a dark bag can see why the light [are|is|'The light' is singular, so use 'is'.] useful.

title: Three pictures for the pool
text: In the first picture, a child [put|puts|'A child' is singular, so add -s: puts.] on a swimming cap. In the next, she walks to the water with her teacher. The last picture shows her in the pool. The pictures [helps|help|'The pictures' is plural, so use 'help'.] new swimmers see what they will do at a lesson. This may make the first visit [feels|feel|After 'make the visit', use the base verb: feel.] easier.

title: The sign on the library door
text: ‘Borrow books here’ is [writen|written|Spelling: 'written' has double t.] in blue on the library door. Next to the words, a picture shows a bag full of books. The bag helps explain the idea. [Childrens|Children|'Children' is already plural: no -s.] can take books home, read them and bring [they|them|After a verb, use 'them', not 'they'.] back. This may make a child want to go in and choose a book.

title: A smile in the dentist’s window
text: [Their|There|'There is' tells us something exists.] is a photo of a smiling girl in the dentist’s window. She sits in a big chair and [hold|holds|'She' takes -s: she holds.] a small mirror. The room looks light and [warmly|warm|After 'looks', use adjectives: light and warm.]. The picture can help a child see what the room is like. A first visit may feel easier after they see the photo.

title: An empty chair by the door
text: A hairdresser puts a picture of [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an empty chair.] empty chair outside the door. The sign says ‘Come in now’. Together, the picture and the words [tells|tell|Two things ('the picture and the words') take 'tell'.] people they do not have to wait. Someone with time before work can go in for a haircut without [make|making|After 'without', use the -ing form: making.] a plan for another day.

title: The first bite of an apple
text: We hear [an|a|Use 'a' before a consonant sound: a loud sound.] loud sound as a girl takes a bite of an apple. Then we see [she|her|After 'see', use 'her', not 'she'.] eat the rest. The sound makes the apple seem [freshly|fresh|After 'seem', use an adjective: fresh.]. People watching the advert can think about how a fresh apple sounds when they eat one. They may want an apple for a snack.

title: The shop with the yellow bags
text: Each [persons|person|After 'each', use a singular noun: person.] in the advert carries the same yellow shopping bag. One gets on a bus and another [walk|walks|'Another' is singular, so add -s: walks.] across a park. The [shops|shop’s|Use an apostrophe to show the name belongs to the shop: shop’s.] name is on every bag. People see the yellow bag again and again. They may know which shop it comes from the next time they see one in town.

title: The cake in the shop door
text: The bakery has a picture of a cake at the same [hight|height|Spelling: 'height' has an e: height.] as a child’s face. The cake [have|has|'The cake' is singular, so use 'has'.] a big smile made of fruit. Children can see the smile as they walk past. A child may stop to look and ask [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an adult.] adult to come in and see the real cake.

title: A little fan on a hot bus
text: People on the bus [is|are|'People' is plural, so use 'are'.] hot. A man wipes [him|his|Use 'his' to show the face belongs to him.] face with his hand. Next to him, a girl takes a small fan out of her pocket. When she turns it on, her hair [move|moves|'Her hair' is singular, so add -s: moves.]. We can see what the fan does. People on the bus may want something that small to keep them cool.

title: A key that is easy to find
text: A pile of silver keys [lie|lies|The subject is 'a pile' (singular), so use 'lies'.] on a table. One key has a bright pink ring. A hand [reachs|reaches|Add -es after -ch: reaches.] for that key at once. The colour shows why the ring is useful. People who spend time looking for the [write|right|'Right' means correct; 'write' is what you do with a pen.] key may want a bright ring for the one they use most.

title: The button under the picture of the cat
text: On a website, a photo shows a cat with [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] eyes closed. A small box below it says ‘See more cats’. A person looking for a pet [know|knows|'A person' is singular, so add -s: knows.] what will happen when they press it. The website makes it [easily|easy|After 'makes it', use an adjective: easy.] to take one more step after a picture gets the person’s attention.

title: A chair that folds flat
text: Two [peoples|people|'People' is already plural: no -s.] sit on chairs in a small garden. After lunch, one person [fold|folds|'One person' is singular, so add -s: folds.] both chairs and puts them by the wall. There is room for the children to play. The advert shows why chairs that fold [is|are|'Chairs' is plural, so use 'are'.] useful. A person with a small garden can use the same place for different things.

title: The clock in the shoe shop
text: A sign in a shoe shop says ‘We close at eight on Fridays’. Next to the words is a picture of a clock. The hands [shows|show|'The hands' is plural, so use 'show'.] eight o’clock. People can see the time without reading every word. A person who [work|works|'A person' is singular, so add -s: works.] late may decide to look for shoes [in|on|We say 'on the way home'.] the way home.

title: The bakery door at seven
text: The shop door is open, and a clock above it [show|shows|'A clock' is singular, so add -s: shows.] seven in the morning. A baker puts hot rolls on a tray near the window. People on [there|their|'Their' means 'belonging to them'.] way to work can see that the bakery is open early. They may stop for a [role|roll|A 'roll' is bread; a 'role' is a part in a play.] before they get on the bus.

title: The blue bowl for soup
text: A blue bowl sits on a table beside a bowl that is plain white. Both [holds|hold|'Both' is plural, so use 'hold'.] the same soup. The blue bowl makes the orange [soap|soup|'Soup' is food; 'soap' is for washing.] look bright. The advert wants people to notice the bowl, so it puts two bowls together. A shopper can see which one looks [gooder|better|The comparative of 'good' is 'better'.] at home.

title: The quiet table in the library
text: The library poster shows one table by a window. A student sits there with a book and a glass of water. There [is|are|'Phones' is plural, so use 'are'.] no phones or [loudly|loud|Use the adjective 'loud' before a noun.] people in the picture. The room looks like a good place to [studying|study|After 'a place to', use the base verb: study.]. Someone who finds it hard to work at home may want to go there.

title: A box that can be a house
text: A toy box has a door and two [window|windows|After 'two', use a plural noun: windows.] printed on it. In the advert, a child takes out the [toys|toy|Before another noun, 'toy' stays singular: toy animals.] animals. Then she turns the empty box into their house. The box is now part of the game. Parents can see that a child can play with more [then|than|Use 'than' to compare.] the toys inside.

title: Flowers for a Monday
text: A woman [come|comes|'A woman' is singular, so add -s: comes.] home on a Monday and finds flowers on the kitchen table. The words say ‘You do not need a special day’. This tells people they can give flowers at any time. Someone watching may think of a friend who [have|has|'A friend' is singular, so use 'has'.] had a difficult [weak|week|'Week' is seven days; 'weak' means not strong.] and want to buy flowers for them.

title: The last piece of a puzzle
text: The advert shows a boy holding one puzzle [peace|piece|A 'piece' is a part of something; 'peace' means calm.]. He puts it in the empty space, and the picture of a boat is complete. His sister smiles and [point|points|'His sister' is singular, so add -s: points.] at it. The last piece gives the children a happy moment. A parent can imagine [do|doing|After 'imagine', use the -ing form: doing.] the same puzzle with a child at home.

title: A round mirror for the hall
text: In the first picture, the hall [have|has|'The hall' is singular, so use 'has'.] an empty wall. In the second, a round mirror is on it. The mirror shows light from a window. [This|These|Use 'these' with a plural noun: these pictures.] pictures help shoppers see the room before and after. Someone with a dark hall may want a mirror to make it [feels|feel|After 'make it', use the base verb: feel.] brighter.

title: The drink in the clear glass
text: The café puts a pink drink in a clear glass. We can see pieces of strawberry at the bottom. The picture shows what is in the drink without [much|many|Use 'many' with plural nouns like 'words'.] words. People who [likes|like|'People' is plural, so use 'like'.] [strawberrys|strawberries|The plural of 'strawberry' is 'strawberries'.] may want to try it. The colour also makes it easy to find on the menu.

title: The bread at the bus stop
text: A poster at the bus stop shows a sandwich with warm bread and cheese. The bakery is on the next street, and an arrow [point|points|'An arrow' is singular, so add -s: points.] that way. People waiting for the bus can see the food and the [shortly|short|Use the adjective 'short' before a noun.] walk to get it. Someone who missed [brekfast|breakfast|Spelling: 'breakfast' starts with 'break'.] may decide to go there.

title: A cup by the tap
text: The poster shows a child [fill|filling|After 'shows a child', use the -ing form: filling.] a cup at a water tap. Next to the tap, a big sign says ‘Free water here’. People can [sees|see|After 'can', use the base verb: see.] where to get a drink. A family in the park may bring their own cups instead of [buy|buying|After 'of', use the -ing form: buying.] drinks from the shop.

title: The family on the bike
text: A woman rides a bike with a child in a seat behind [she|her|After 'behind', use 'her', not 'she'.]. They pass cars that [is|are|'Cars' is plural, so use 'are'.] waiting at a red light. The child waves at someone on the path. The advert makes the bike ride look [pleasantly|pleasant|After 'look', use an adjective: pleasant.]. A parent who travels a short way to school may think about riding.

title: The blue chair at the cinema
text: A cinema advert shows a child sitting in a wide blue chair. There [are|is|'Room' here means space, which is uncountable, so use 'is'.] room for her coat and a bag of popcorn. She looks up at a big screen. The photo shows what a visit [feel|feels|'A visit' is singular, so add -s: feels.] like. A parent can see that the child [have|has|'The child' is singular, so use 'has'.] a good place to sit.

title: A paper boat on the poster
text: A poster for [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an art class.] art class shows a paper boat in a child’s hand. There are more boats on the table, but they [is|are|'They' takes 'are'.] different colours. The picture shows a simple thing children can make. Someone who likes using paper and colour may want to come and make a boat [to|too|'Too' here means 'also'.].

title: A big clock over the door
text: A clock on a shop poster shows nine in the evening. Under it [is|are|'The words' is plural, so use 'are'.] the words ‘Open late tonight’. People can see the time at once. Someone who cannot shop in the day may see that [their|there|'There is' tells us something exists.] is still time to visit after work and [by|buy|'Buy' means pay for; 'by' means next to.] what they need.

title: A hot bowl after the rain
text: A boy comes into a café with a wet coat. The woman at the counter gives [he|him|After 'gives', use 'him', not 'he'.] a bowl of soup. He holds the bowl with both [hand|hands|After 'both', use a plural noun: hands.] and smiles. The advert makes the soup look [warmly|warm|After 'look', use an adjective: warm.]. People who are cold outside may want to stop and eat some.

title: The basket beside the till
text: A shop puts small packets of seeds beside the till. The sign above them says ‘Flowers for spring’. People see the packets while they [pays|pay|'They' takes 'pay' (no -s).] for other things. Someone who [comed|came|The past of 'come' is 'came'.] in for a plant may buy seeds too because the sign gives them [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an idea.] idea for their garden.

title: The step outside the shop
text: A poster outside a shoe shop shows a woman stepping into a [deeply|deep|Use the adjective 'deep' before a noun.] puddle. Her new shoes [stays|stay|'Her new shoes' is plural, so use 'stay'.] dry. The puddle gives the shoes a job to do in the picture. People walking in the rain can see why they might need shoes like these before [go|going|After 'before', use the -ing form: going.] home that day.

title: The white line on a dark road
text: In the bike light advert, a rider [go|goes|'A rider' is singular, so add -s: goes.] along a dark street. The light shows a wide white line on the [rode|road|A 'road' is a street; 'rode' is the past of 'ride'.] ahead. The rider can see where to go. People who ride home after sunset may look at the line and think about using a light [theirselves|themselves|The correct word is 'themselves'.].

title: An open door on the school poster
text: The poster shows a teacher standing in [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an open door.] open classroom door. Inside, children [works|work|'Children' is plural, so use 'work'.] in small groups at tables. The door lets parents see part of the school day. The teacher [look|looks|'The teacher' is singular, so add -s: looks.] ready to welcome someone in. A family looking for a new school may want to visit soon.

title: The boy with the blue balloon
text: On the party shop’s poster, a boy [hold|holds|'A boy' is singular, so add -s: holds.] one blue balloon. Behind him are [much|many|Use 'many' with plural nouns.] other balloons in different colours. The single balloon helps people see [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] shape, and the ones behind show the choice in the shop. A family planning a party may come in to choose colours.

title: A banana in the bag
text: A boy [open|opens|'A boy' is singular, so add -s: opens.] his school bag after a long day. His banana is still in one [peace|piece|A 'piece' is a part of something; 'peace' means calm.] inside a little box. The advert shows the box doing one simple job. A parent who puts fruit in a school bag may like a way to keep it from [get|getting|After 'from', use the -ing form: getting.] hurt.

title: The first bite of a sandwich
text: In a food advert, a woman opens a paper bag on the train. She takes a bite of her sandwich and looks out [off|of|We say 'out of' the window.] the window. Other people [sits|sit|'People' is plural, so use 'sit'.] with empty hands. The scene makes the sandwich look like a good thing to take on a journey, [especialy|especially|Spelling: 'especially' has double l.] when it is time for lunch.

title: The umbrella that covers two
text: Two friends walk in the rain under one large [umbrela|umbrella|Spelling: 'umbrella' has double l.]. They both stay dry, and there is still room for [there|their|'Their' means 'belonging to them'.] bags. This shows the size of the umbrella better [then|than|Use 'than' to compare.] a number on a label. Someone who often walks with a friend may want to buy one this big.

title: The dog by the shop door
text: A dog waits outside a shop while [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] owner buys food. A little bowl of water [are|is|The subject is 'a bowl' (singular), so use 'is'.] beside the door. The poster shows the bowl with the words ‘Water for dogs’. Dog owners may notice that their pets can [has|have|After 'can', use the base verb: have.] a drink. They may feel happy to stop at the shop.

title: The hot bread beside the clock
text: A clock on the bakery sign shows eight. Beside it, a picture shows hot bread coming out of [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an oven.] oven. The words say ‘Fresh at eight’. A person on the way to work can see when the bread [are|is|'Bread' is uncountable, so use 'is'.] ready. They may walk [passed|past|'Past' here means 'going by'; 'passed' is a verb.] at that time to buy a warm loaf.

title: One red book on the shelf
text: Many grey books [stands|stand|'Books' is plural, so use 'stand'.] on a shelf, but one book is red. The advert puts the red book in the middle. It is the first thing we see. People may remember the colour when they [goes|go|'They' takes 'go' (no -s).] to the shop. The picture helps [they|them|After 'helps', use 'them', not 'they'.] find the same book among many others.

title: A red bike with a bell
text: A small red bike is in the middle of the advert. A boy rings its bell before he [ride|rides|'He' takes -s: he rides.] past his friend. The sound makes the friend [turns|turn|After 'makes the friend', use the base verb: turn.] and smile. The advert lets [childrens|children|'Children' is already plural: no -s.] hear one part of the bike. They may want to try the bell at the shop.

title: The jacket on the hook
text: A child comes in from the rain and [hang|hangs|'A child' is singular, so add -s: hangs.] a wet jacket on a hook. Water [fall|falls|'Water' is singular, so add -s: falls.] onto a tray below. The poster shows both the hook and the tray. A family can see where wet clothes will [goes|go|After 'will', use the base verb: go.]. They may want one near the door at home.

title: The new path through the park
text: On a poster, a thin blue line [go|goes|'A line' is singular, so add -s: goes.] from the park gate to the lake. The words say ‘New path now open’. People can see where the path goes. A visitor who [want|wants|'A visitor' is singular, so add -s: wants.] to see the lake may come to the park and [follows|follow|After 'may come and', use the base verb: follow.] the line on the map.

title: The dog in the car
text: A dog sits on a mat in the back of a car. After the journey, the owner [take|takes|'The owner' is singular, so add -s: takes.] out the mat. The seat under it is clean. The advert shows why the mat [matter|matters|'The mat' is singular, so add -s: matters.]. A person who takes a dog on walks may want to keep mud [of|off|'Off' means away from; 'of' shows belonging.] the car seats.

title: A small box for a big gift
text: A child opens a small gift box and [find|finds|'A child' is singular, so add -s: finds.] a card for a day at the zoo. The next picture shows [she|her|After 'shows', use 'her', not 'she'.] looking at a giraffe. The advert shows that the gift is a trip, even [thought|though|'Though' means 'although'; 'thought' is the past of 'think'.] the box is small. A parent may want to give a day out as a present.

title: The number on the birthday candle
text: A cake has one candle shaped like the number six. Behind it [is|are|'Candles' is plural, so use 'are'.] candles with other numbers. The shop shows that families can [chooses|choose|After 'can', use the base verb: choose.] the number they need. A parent planning a birthday can see what to buy. The picture also makes the cake look ready [to|for|We say 'ready for' something: ready for a party.] a party.

title: The picture at the end of the lesson
text: A child [start|starts|'A child' is singular, so add -s: starts.] a drawing with a small blue circle. At the end of the art lesson, the circle is the centre of a big flower. The advert shows the start and the [finish|finished|Use 'finished' (completed) before 'picture'.] picture. A beginner can see that a picture can grow from one [simply|simple|Use the adjective 'simple' before a noun.] shape on the page.

title: A cold drink on a hot day
text: In the poster, drops of water [covers|cover|The subject is 'drops' (plural), so use 'cover'.] the outside of a bottle. Behind it, the sun shines on a busy street. The bottle looks cold, and the street looks hot. This makes the drink look [well|good|After 'look', use the adjective 'good'.] to people [walked|walking|Use the -ing form: people (who are) walking home.] home in the sun. They can almost feel the cold bottle in their hands.

title: A museum on a rainy day
text: Rain falls outside a museum, but the people in the poster are inside and smiling. A little boy points up at a large dinosaur. His face shows how [exciting|excited|Use 'excited' for the person who has the feeling.] he is. A parent who [need|needs|'A parent' is singular, so add -s: needs.] somewhere to take the children on a wet day can picture them [enjoy|enjoying|After 'picture them', use the -ing form: enjoying.] a visit there.

title: The orange juice sound
text: First we hear an orange [been|being|Use 'being' for something happening now: being cut.] cut. Then we hear juice going into a glass. The name of the drink comes [in|at|'At the end' means at the final point: at the end of the advert.] the end of the radio advert. The sounds [helps|help|'The sounds' is plural, so use 'help'.] listeners picture fruit in a kitchen. They may expect the drink in the bottle to taste like juice they make at home.

title: The bookshop stamp card
text: A sign at the bookshop says, ‘Buy five books and get your sixth book free.’ Next to the words, there [are|is|'A picture' is singular, so use 'is'.] a picture of a card with five [stamp|stamps|After 'five', use a plural noun: stamps.] on it. The picture shows customers how to get the free book. It also gives people who [reads|read|'People' is plural, so use 'read'.] a lot a reason to shop there again.

title: A small box of tools
text: Each tool in the advert has [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] own place in the box. One place is empty, and a hand puts the last tool back. This shows how [easily|easy|After 'it is', use the adjective: how easy it is.] it is to see when something is missing. People who often [loose|lose|'Lose' means you cannot find something; 'loose' means not tight.] things around the house may like the idea of keeping all their tools together.

title: The football club’s open day
text: A poster shows two boys and two girls playing football on the same team. Under the picture, the club has [wrote|written|The past participle of 'write' is 'written'.] ‘Come and play’. The people in the picture [helps|help|'The people' is plural, so use 'help'.] show who the message is for. A girl who would like to play may feel more welcome when she [see|sees|'She' takes -s: she sees.] girls on the team.

title: A poster for a lost pet service
text: ‘She came home on Friday’ appears under a photo of a cat asleep in its own bed. The line [tell|tells|'The line' is singular, so add -s: tells.] people how the story ended before they read about the service. The safe, [slept|sleeping|Use the -ing form: a sleeping cat.] cat gives them hope. Someone who has [lose|lost|After 'has', use the past participle: lost.] a pet may feel ready to ask the service for help.

title: A hotel with breakfast included
text: The hotel advert shows a table with eggs, toast and fruit. Next to the table, it says ‘Breakfast included’. The words [tells|tell|'The words' is plural, so use 'tell'.] guests that the room [prize|price|A 'price' is what you pay; a 'prize' is what you win.] also pays for the food. This can make the hotel look like a better choice for a family, [specially|especially|Use 'especially' to mean 'in particular'.] if they would usually pay for breakfast somewhere else.

title: The swimming bag under the bench
text: In the advert, a child [put|puts|'A child' is singular, so add -s: puts.] a wet towel in one side of a swimming bag and dry clothes in the other. At the end, she takes out a dry shirt. Seeing both sides [help|helps|'Seeing…' is one action, so use 'helps'.] viewers understand the point of the bag. Parents may like the idea of [keep|keeping|After 'of', use the -ing form: keeping.] clean clothes dry after a swim.

title: A photo album for Grandma
text: In the advert, a woman opens a photo album and finds a picture of her [grandchilds|grandchildren|The plural of 'child' is 'children': grandchildren.] at the beach. She laughs when she sees their faces covered [of|in|We say 'covered in' or 'covered with' sand.] sand. The advert shows why the album might make a good gift. A viewer can imagine [give|giving|After 'imagine', use the -ing form: giving.] someone a book full of moments that they enjoyed together.

title: The barber’s chair
text: A young boy sits in the barber’s chair with a toy train in his hands. The barber waits for him to finish [play|playing|After 'finish', use the -ing form: playing.] before asking him to sit still. Showing what happens before the haircut makes the barber look kind and [patience|patient|After 'look', use adjectives: kind and patient.]. Parents [who's|whose|'Whose' shows possession; 'who's' means 'who is'.] children are worried about haircuts may feel more comfortable booking there.

title: A new bag from old jeans
text: First the camera shows a pair of jeans with a [whole|hole|A 'hole' is an empty space; 'whole' means all of something.] in the knee. Then it shows a bag made [by|from|Use 'made from' for the material something is made of.] the same blue cloth. We can still see the pocket from the jeans on the front. This detail makes the change [easily|easy|After 'makes the change', use the adjective: easy.] to follow. People who like to reuse old things may want to learn how to make one.

title: The menu in the window
text: A café puts pictures of its lunch dishes in the window. Each photo [have|has|'Each photo' is singular, so use 'has'.] the price right below it. A person walking past can see what looks good and how [many|much|Use 'how much' for a price.] it costs before going inside. That may help someone decide to stop, especially if they are in a hurry or have only a [few|little|Use 'a little' with uncountable nouns like 'money'.] money to spend.

title: A simple meal for one
text: An advert for a [freezed|frozen|The past participle of 'freeze' is 'frozen'.] meal shows a single plate and a fork on a small table. The food pack beside it says ‘Serves one’. The scene shows exactly how much food [come|comes|'Food' is uncountable, so add -s: comes.] in the pack. A person who [cook|cooks|'A person' is singular, so add -s: cooks.] only for themselves can see that they will have enough for dinner without food left over.

title: A cake for a small party
text: Two cakes appear in the bakery advert. One is tall and has [much|many|Use 'many' with plural nouns like 'pieces'.] pieces. The other is small and has just four. Showing the two sizes side by side helps people choose. Someone planning a birthday tea with a [little|few|Use 'a few' with plural nouns like 'friends'.] friends can see that they can buy a cake without [have|having|After 'without', use the -ing form: having.] lots left over.

title: The red umbrella in the crowd
text: People hurry [passed|past|'Past' here means 'going by'; 'passed' is a verb.] the camera with plain black umbrellas. A woman opens a red one, and her friend spots [she|her|After a verb, use 'her', not 'she'.] at once. The advert uses the crowd to show how [differently|different|After 'looks', use the adjective: different.] the red umbrella looks. A shopper who wants something easy to find in a busy place may remember the red umbrella when they next need one.

title: No trips to the post office
text: In an advert for a parcel service, a driver takes a box from someone at their front door. Behind the customer, we can see two more [box|boxes|After 'two more', use a plural noun: boxes.] ready to go. The short scene shows that people can send parcels without [leave|leaving|After 'without', use the -ing form: leaving.] home. This may appeal to someone who [have|has|'Someone' is singular, so use 'has'.] several heavy boxes to send and no car.

title: A ticket for an empty seat
text: An advert for a concert shows one empty seat in the middle of a happy crowd. The words ‘Your place is waiting’ [appears|appear|'The words' is plural, so use 'appear'.] above it. The empty seat lets viewers picture [theirselves|themselves|The correct word is 'themselves'.] at the show. Someone who enjoys live music may feel that the advert is asking them [personal|personally|Use the adverb 'personally' to describe how it asks.] to come along.

title: The train card beside a calendar
text: A train company shows a travel card next to a [calender|calendar|Spelling: 'calendar' ends in -ar.]. Every weekday [have|has|'Every weekday' is singular, so use 'has'.] a small blue mark, but the weekends are left clear. The marks help people see when they could use the card. Someone who [take|takes|'Someone' is singular, so add -s: takes.] the same train to work may compare the offer with what they usually spend.

title: The café chair with a coat on it
text: A coat [hang|hangs|'A coat' is singular, so add -s: hangs.] over a chair in the café photograph. A cup and an open laptop [sits|sit|Two things ('a cup and a laptop') take 'sit'.] on the table, but nobody is in the picture. This gives viewers space to imagine sitting there themselves. Someone looking for a [quite|quiet|'Quiet' means not noisy; 'quite' means 'fairly'.] place to work may see that the café has room for them.

title: One button for the whole room
text: A light advert shows a family leaving home. The father [press|presses|'The father' is singular, so add -es: presses.] one button by the door, and all the lights [goes|go|'The lights' is plural, so use 'go'.] out. The scene shows why the button could be useful. People who often walk back through their house to check the lights may like [be|being|After 'like' here, use the -ing form: being able.] able to turn them off at once.

title: A small garden on a tall building
text: The advert shows a few pots on a flat roof, high above the busy streets. A woman picks a [tomatoe|tomato|Spelling: 'tomato' has no e at the end.] and carries it inside. The setting shows that a garden does not [needs|need|After 'does not', use the base verb: need.] a large piece of land. People [lived|living|Use the -ing form: people (who are) living in flats.] in flats may imagine growing food on a roof or balcony of their own.

title: The beach clean-up gloves
text: A beach poster shows hands wearing gloves as they pick up plastic near the water. The [peoples|people’s|Use an apostrophe to show the faces belong to the people: people’s.] faces [is|are|'Faces' is plural, so use 'are'.] outside the picture. This puts the work at the centre of the advert and helps viewers imagine doing it themselves. Someone who wants to help can see that joining [begin|begins|'Joining' is one action, so add -s: begins.] with a simple action.

title: A map on the museum floor
text: The museum advert shows a coloured line [runing|running|Spelling: double the n: running.] across the floor. Children [follows|follow|'Children' is plural, so use 'follow'.] it from a dinosaur to a large ship. The line helps them find their way through the building. A parent who worries that a large museum will be difficult to visit may see [a|an|Use 'an' before a vowel sound: an easier way.] easier way to explore it.

title: A bag that stands on its own
text: A student puts her bag on the classroom floor and [take|takes|'A student' is singular, so add -s: takes.] out a book. The bag stays upright, so she can see what is inside. The advert shows this small detail [while|during|Use 'during' before a noun; 'while' goes before a clause.] an ordinary school day. Students who often have to search through a [fell|fallen|Use the past participle 'fallen' before a noun.] bag may see why this one could help.

title: The library card with a picture
text: An advert for the library shows a child holding [an|a|Use 'a' before a consonant sound: a new card.] new card with her own picture on it. She uses the card to take home a book about space. The photo makes the card feel like something that [belong|belongs|'Something' is singular, so add -s: belongs.] to her. Other children may want a card so they can [chose|choose|After 'can', use the base verb 'choose'; 'chose' is the past.] books for themselves.

title: The food photo from above
text: A café [does|takes|We say 'take a photo'.] a photo of lunch from above. We can see the rice, vegetables and egg on one plate, with nothing [hid|hidden|Use the past participle 'hidden'.] behind another item. This angle helps customers know what they will get. Someone choosing food from a website may order more [easy|easily|Use the adverb 'easily' to describe how they order.] when they can see the whole meal.

title: The button on the winter coat
text: In the video, a girl pulls her hands inside the sleeves of a coat. She closes a button at each [wrists|wrist|After 'each', use a singular noun: wrist.], so the sleeves [stays|stay|'The sleeves' is plural, so use 'stay'.] around her hands. The close shot shows exactly how the buttons [works|work|'The buttons' is plural, so use 'work'.]. Parents looking for a coat for cold school mornings may notice this detail.

title: A blue box under the bed
text: An advert for a storage box shows a family clearing toys from the floor. They put them in a blue box and [slid|slide|Keep to the present tense: they put … and slide.] it under the bed. The room looks [largest|larger|Use the comparative 'larger' to compare two moments.] when the floor is clear. Parents with a small bedroom may see that the box gives them a way to use space they [yet|already|'Already' means before now; 'yet' is used in questions and negatives.] have.

title: The chair beside the window
text: In the [furnitures|furniture|'Furniture' is uncountable: no -s.] advert, a chair sits by a window with a pile of books next to it. Sunlight [reach|reaches|'Sunlight' is singular, so add -es: reaches.] the seat. The room looks ready for someone to read there. Shoppers can picture how the chair might fit into a quiet part of their own home, even if they have never [saw|seen|After 'have', use the past participle: seen.] the room before.

title: The number at the end of the race
text: After a school race, a boy looks at the number on his watch. The advert does not show where he finished. It shows that he ran faster [then|than|Use 'than' to compare.] on his last try. This may appeal to children who like to see their own [progresses|progress|'Progress' is uncountable: no -s.], even when they do not [won|win|After 'do not', use the base verb: win.] a race.

title: The garden game on the phone
text: A phone game advert shows a girl moving flowers into a garden. At the end, she [send|sends|'She' takes -s: she sends.] a picture of her garden to a friend. The advert makes building the garden look [relaxed|relaxing|Use 'relaxing' for the thing that makes you calm.] and sharing it look fun. Someone who likes simple games may want to try [make|making|After 'try', use the -ing form here: try making.] a different garden.

title: A bright button on the holiday page
text: Pictures of [beachs|beaches|Add -es after -ch: beaches.] fill most of the holiday website. Below each picture is a bright button with the words ‘Check dates’. A visitor can [chooses|choose|After 'can', use the base verb: choose.] a place first and then see when they can go. The buttons make it [easily|easy|After 'make it', use an adjective: easy.] to move from imagining a trip to planning it.

title: The first word in the language lesson
text: A learner says ‘hello’ to the camera. The teacher answers [slow|slowly|Use the adverb 'slowly' to describe how the teacher answers.] and asks a simple question. The advert shows a short conversation instead of a list of lessons. Someone who is nervous about [speak|speaking|After 'about', use the -ing form: speaking.] a new language may see that the first exchange can [began|begin|After 'can', use the base verb: begin.] with only one word.

title: The dinner plate with a line
text: A plate in the advert has a [colour|coloured|Use 'coloured' (an adjective) before 'line'.] line around the middle. A cook puts rice on one side and vegetables on the other. The line shows how [many|much|Use 'how much' with uncountable nouns like 'space'.] space each food [take|takes|'Each food' is singular, so add -s: takes.]. People planning a meal can see how the plate might help them put different kinds of food together.

title: The shop’s repair promise
text: A shop window has a sign saying ‘We fix what we sell’. Under it [are|is|'A photo' is singular, so use 'is'.] a photo of someone repairing a jacket. The words [gives|give|'The words' is plural, so use 'give'.] shoppers a promise, and the photo shows what the work looks like. A customer who wants clothes to last may feel [gooder|better|The comparative of 'good' is 'better'.] about buying from this shop.

title: The video that starts with a question
text: ‘Where do your old batteries go?’ appears on screen while a hand holds two [use|used|Use 'used' (old) before 'batteries'.] batteries. The video then shows a box for them at a shop. Beginning with a question makes viewers [thinks|think|After 'makes viewers', use the base verb: think.] about what they do at home. The answer gives [they|them|After 'gives', use 'them', not 'they'.] a place to take the batteries next time.

title: The candle that lights the picture
text: In a [darkly|dark|Use the adjective 'dark' before a noun.] room, someone [light|lights|'Someone' is singular, so add -s: lights.] a candle next to a photo of friends. The light [make|makes|'The light' is singular, so add -s: makes.] the faces in the photo easier to see. The advert links the candle to a quiet moment at home. A viewer may imagine using it when they want the room to feel calm.

title: The same smile on two posters
text: One poster shows a grandmother smiling at her grandson. Another shows the grandson smiling at a video call with her. Both posters [advertises|advertise|'Both posters' is plural, so use 'advertise'.] the same phone service. The [repeating|repeated|Use 'repeated' (shown again) for the smile.] smile connects them, even though the family is in different places. Viewers may think about people they want to [speaking|speak|After 'want to', use the base verb: speak.] to.

title: One window, two seasons
text: A window advert shows the same room in summer and winter. In summer, sunlight [fill|fills|'Sunlight' is singular, so add -s: fills.] it. In winter, a family sits near the window while snow falls outside. The room stays [comfortably|comfortable|After 'stays', use the adjective: comfortable.] in both pictures. Customers who are choosing new windows can think about using them through the [hole|whole|'Whole' means all of something; a 'hole' is an empty space.] year.

title: A simple sign for new students
text: At the front of a school, a sign [have|has|'A sign' is singular, so use 'has'.] an arrow and the words ‘New students this way’. The advert for the school shows a family [followed|following|After 'shows a family', use the -ing form: following.] it to a teacher. The sign makes the first visit [easyer|easier|Spelling: 'easy' becomes 'easier'.] to picture. A child who is nervous about a new school can see where to go.

title: The coat that leaves room
text: An advert shows a child wearing a coat over a thick school jumper. The child can still move both [arm|arms|After 'both', use a plural noun: arms.] and reach for a ball. This helps parents see how the coat [fit|fits|'The coat' is singular, so add -s: fits.] with winter clothes. A coat may look good on [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] own, but families need it to work over other things too.

title: The little hand on the clock
text: A watch advert shows a child learning to [reading|read|After 'to', use the base verb: read.] the time. A large clock face [fill|fills|'A large clock face' is singular, so add -s: fills.] the screen as a parent points to the short hand. The close view lets children follow the lesson. Parents can see how the clear numbers on the watch might [helps|help|After 'might', use the base verb: help.] a child learn.

title: The clock on the washing machine
text: A woman puts clothes in the machine before she leaves [to|for|We say 'leave for' a place: leaves for work.] work. On her phone, she [choose|chooses|'She' takes -s: she chooses.] a time for it to finish. She comes home when the washing ends. The advert uses her day to show how the timer works. Someone with a busy schedule may find that [usefully|useful|After 'find that', use the adjective: useful.].

title: A cup left on the train
text: The advert begins with a cup [leaved|left|'Left' is the past participle of 'leave'.] on a train seat. A cleaner finds it and puts it in a box at the station. Its owner [come|comes|'Its owner' is singular, so add -s: comes.] back and takes it home. The story shows how the lost property service works. Travellers may [feels|feel|After 'may', use the base verb: feel.] better knowing where to ask if they forget something.

title: A weekend class for parents
text: The cooking [schools|school’s|Use an apostrophe to show the poster belongs to the school: school’s.] poster shows a parent and a child making a meal together. Both [has|have|'Both' is plural, so use 'have'.] [flower|flour|'Flour' is for baking; a 'flower' grows in a garden.] on their hands, and the child is doing some of the work. This shows that the class is for both of them. A parent looking for something to do at the weekend may want to book it.

title: The shoe beside the ruler
text: In a [childrens’|children’s|The plural is 'children', so the possessive is 'children’s'.] shoe advert, a parent puts a child’s foot beside a ruler printed on a sheet. The next shot shows the size to order online. The advert shows how to measure before [buy|buying|After 'before', use the -ing form: buying.]. Parents who cannot visit the shop may feel more able to choose a pair that [fit|fits|'A pair' is singular, so add -s: fits.].

title: A school jumper that stays bright
text: The advert shows a red school jumper after many [washs|washes|Add -es after -sh: washes.]. Beside it [are|is|'A new one' is singular, so use 'is'.] a new one in the same colour. By [put|putting|After 'by', use the -ing form: putting.] them together, the shop asks parents to compare them. Parents who wash school clothes often may want a jumper that keeps its colour through the school year.

title: The soup on the shelf at six
text: A shop advert shows soup on a shelf as a clock [reach|reaches|'A clock' is singular, so add -es: reaches.] six in the evening. A person [came|coming|Use the -ing form: a person (who is) coming home.] home from work picks it up. The time helps viewers see when the soup might be useful. People who do not want to cook late may think about [keep|keeping|After 'about', use the -ing form: keeping.] it at home.

title: A place to put your cup
text: At a small desk, a student puts a cup in a round holder on the side. She can move her books without [knock|knocking|After 'without', use the -ing form: knocking.] it over. The advert shows why the holder is useful through her actions. Someone with [few|little|Use 'little' with uncountable nouns like 'space'.] space to work may want a desk that [keep|keeps|'A desk' is singular, so add -s: keeps.] drinks away from papers.

title: A cereal box
text: A cartoon tiger rides a bicycle down a mountain on the front of the cereal box. [It's|Its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] wide grin makes breakfast look like something children might get [exciting|excited|Use 'excited' for the person who has the feeling.] about. Just below the tiger, a [smallest|smaller|Use the comparative 'smaller' (smaller than the tiger).] label says ‘High in fibre’. This gives parents a [difference|different|Use the adjective 'different' before a noun.] reason to choose the cereal when their children spot the box and ask for it.

title: A backpack in the rain
text: The backpack advert shows a benefit that [matter|matters|'A benefit' is singular, so add -s: matters.] to people who cycle to work. Rain runs down the bag [while|during|Use 'during' before a noun; 'while' goes before a clause.] the journey, but the papers inside are still dry when the cyclist reaches the office. By showing [that|those|Use 'those' with a plural noun: those papers.] papers at the end, the advert gives viewers a clear way to judge the bag’s performance. They can imagine arriving at work with their own things [protecting|protected|Use the past participle: things (that are) protected.].

title: The missing car keys
text: A radio advert for a key finder begins with the sound of drawers opening and a bus pulling away. Then a short beep [led|leads|Keep to the present tense: the advert begins … a beep leads.] the speaker to the keys under a cushion. Listeners can follow the search [though|through|'Through' means 'by means of'; 'though' means 'although'.] sound alone. Anyone who has been late because they lost their keys can hear how the product would change a morning they know [good|well|Use the adverb 'well': they know it well.].

title: Soup after the match
text: At the start of the soup advert, a boy comes home from a football match with wet socks and [muds|mud|'Mud' is uncountable: no -s.] on his legs. When he takes his first spoonful, the picture moves in close to the steam [raising|rising|'Rise' has no object; 'raise' needs one (raise your hand).] from his bowl. The change from cold rain to a warm kitchen links the soup with the [relieve|relief|'Relief' is the noun; 'relieve' is the verb.] of being home after a miserable afternoon outside.

title: A quiet clean
text: In the vacuum cleaner advert, a child sleeps on the sofa while his father cleans the carpet nearby. The child stays [sleep|asleep|Use the adjective 'asleep' after 'stays'.] even as the cleaner passes close to the sofa. That detail suggests the machine is [quite|quiet|'Quiet' means not noisy; 'quite' means 'fairly'.] enough to use while other people are resting. Parents who have to fit cleaning around a child’s nap may see an [immediately|immediate|Use the adjective 'immediate' before a noun.] benefit.

title: An advert that sounds like a match
text: A drinks advert opens with three sharp sounds: the bounce of a basketball, the squeak of a shoe and the crack of a can opening. The sounds follow the same [rythm|rhythm|Spelling: 'rhythm' starts with 'rh'.], so opening the can [feel|feels|'Opening the can' is one action, so add -s: feels.] like part of the game. Viewers who recognise the noise of an indoor court may begin to connect the drink with the excitement of [play|playing|After 'of', use the -ing form: playing.] there.

title: A suitcase on the stairs
text: The suitcase advert focuses [in|on|We say 'focus on' something.] a problem that travellers often face. At a railway station, a lift is out of order, so a passenger [pick|picks|'A passenger' is singular, so add -s: picks.] up the case and climbs the stairs with one hand free. The station gives viewers a reason to care about the case’s [wait|weight|'Weight' is how heavy something is; 'wait' means stay until something happens.]. They can picture carrying it at a point in the journey [which|when|Use 'when' for a point in time.] the wheels would be no help.

title: The sticker on a fruit box
text: A large ‘Wonky but tasty’ sticker appears on a box of oddly shaped apples. One apple is [many|much|Use 'much' before a comparative: much wider.] wider on one side, but a photograph on the label shows it cut open with clean white flesh inside. The words make the unusual shape sound [playfully|playful|After 'sound', use an adjective: playful.], and the photo addresses a more practical concern. Shoppers can see why the apples might still be worth [buy|buying|After 'worth', use the -ing form: buying.].

title: One drop of washing-up liquid
text: The advert holds on a close-up as a single drop of washing-up liquid [fall|falls|The subject is 'a single drop' (singular), so add -s: falls.] into a bowl. The next shot shows someone cleaning a stack of greasy plates in that water. By drawing attention to the small [number|amount|Use 'amount' with uncountable things like liquid.] used, the advert suggests that one bottle could [lasts|last|After 'could', use the base verb: last.] for many washes. This may matter to shoppers who think about how often they have to replace it.

title: Room for a friend
text: An advert for a sofa shows two people at opposite [end|ends|Two people sit at two ends, so use the plural: opposite ends.], with a dog asleep in the middle. By putting all three in the frame, the photograph gives viewers an idea of how much space the sofa [offer|offers|'The sofa' is singular, so add -s: offers.]. The scene also helps them picture it in use. The empty area around the dog looks like somewhere a visitor could sit without [someone|anyone|After 'without', use 'anyone'.] having to move.

title: Lunch at the touch of a button
text: The food delivery advert says ‘Order again’ above a picture of last [weeks|week’s|Use an apostrophe: last week’s lunch.] lunch. Under it, there is a single button. A repeat customer can see that they can get the same meal without [search|searching|After 'without', use the -ing form: searching.] the menu or entering their order again. Putting that option at the top of the screen [make|makes|'Putting that option…' is one action, so use 'makes'.] the service look useful to someone with a short lunch break.

title: The toothbrush with two lights
text: A toothpaste advert might focus on a bright smile, but this toothbrush advert shows a child trying to get ready for school. A red light on the brush [turn|turns|'A red light' is singular, so add -s: turns.] green when she has [brush|brushed|After 'has', use the past participle: brushed.] for long enough. That small change shows why the brush could help at home. It gives the child a [clearly|clear|Use the adjective 'clear' before a noun.] signal and gives the parent one less thing to check.

title: A holiday that starts with silence
text: The travel advert spends its first few seconds showing [crowding|crowded|Use 'crowded' (full of people).] pavements and ringing phones. Then it cuts to a still lake, [which|where|Use 'where' for a place.] the only sound is a paddle touching the water. The sudden quiet makes the lake feel [peacefully|peaceful|After 'feel', use an adjective: peaceful.] before the name of the resort appears. For viewers who spend their day in [noise|noisy|Use the adjective 'noisy' before 'places'.] places, the sound of the lake could be a reason to book.

title: Chocolate in the office drawer
text: A chocolate advert follows a woman as she closes her laptop and opens a drawer. Inside [are|is|'A single square' is singular, so use 'is'.] a single square of chocolate, [wrapping|wrapped|Use the past participle: a square (that is) wrapped.] in gold paper. The close-up makes unwrapping it feel like a small event. The advert presents the chocolate as a reward that [fit|fits|'A reward' is singular, so add -s: fits.] into an ordinary day, which may appeal to someone looking for a treat they can give themselves after work.

title: The jeans with deep pockets
text: ‘Yes, your phone fits’ is printed beside a photo of a phone [tucking|tucked|Use the past participle: a phone (that is) tucked.] all the way into a jeans pocket. The word ‘yes’ [sound|sounds|'The word' is singular, so add -s: sounds.] like an answer to a question customers already ask. That makes the advert feel as if it understands a common [frustrating|frustration|Use the noun 'frustration' after 'a common'.]. Shoppers who have had to carry their phones by hand may see the deeper pocket as a good reason to switch brands.

title: A garden in a shoebox
text: The advert for a seed kit shows a small cardboard box on a balcony, with green [leafs|leaves|The plural of 'leaf' is 'leaves'.] growing over [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] edges. Behind it, we can see the windows of other flats. The setting is important because it shows who could use the kit. Someone who [live|lives|'Someone' is singular, so add -s: lives.] high above the street can imagine growing a [little|few|Use 'a few' with plural nouns like 'herbs'.] herbs without having a garden.

title: A poster at the swimming pool
text: ‘One lane just for beginners’ appears above a photograph of adults standing in the shallow end. The people in the picture are listening to a teacher, and one of them is holding a float. [This|These|Use 'these' with a plural noun: these details.] details make it easier to imagine [join|joining|After 'imagine', use the -ing form: joining.] the class as a beginner. An adult who [feel|feels|'An adult' is singular, so add -s: feels.] nervous about learning to swim can see that other people are starting at the same point.

title: A sign that appears at lunchtime
text: A café changes the picture on its outside screen at midday. The morning coffee [give|gives|'The morning coffee' is singular, so add -s: gives.] way to a bowl of hot noodles, and the price appears beside it. People who pass [in|on|We say 'on their lunch break'.] their lunch break see food they can buy now. Showing the right meal at the right time may turn a [quickly|quick|Use the adjective 'quick' before a noun.] look into a visit.

title: The bottle at the end of the run
text: For most of the video, the sports bottle [stay|stays|'The sports bottle' is singular, so add -s: stays.] in a runner’s bag. We see it only when she stops to rest and [need|needs|'She' takes -s: she needs.] a drink. This gives the product a natural place in her day. Viewers who run may find the scene [believeable|believable|Spelling: 'believable' drops the e of 'believe'.] because they know how good water feels after exercise.

title: A spare battery in the drawer
text: In the advert, a camera [looses|loses|'Lose' means no longer have; 'loose' means not tight.] power just as a child [blow|blows|'A child' is singular, so add -s: blows.] out birthday candles. The father opens a drawer and finds a spare battery. The next shot shows the child smiling in a photo. The story connects the battery with a moment the family wants to remember, making it seem worth [have|having|After 'worth', use the -ing form: having.] ready at home.

title: A phone screen in the sun
text: A woman tries to read a message outside, but the sunlight makes her old screen [hardly|hard|'Hard' is the adjective here; 'hardly' means 'almost not'.] to see. She moves into the shade. In the next shot, she reads the same message on the advertised phone while [stay|staying|After 'while', use the -ing form: staying.] in the sun. This [directly|direct|Use the adjective 'direct' before a noun.] comparison makes the brighter screen useful in a familiar situation.

title: The same shoes on different feet
text: Three people wear the same style of shoes in different colours. One walks to work, another [go|goes|'Another' is singular, so add -es: goes.] to college and the third meets friends. The advert shows how the shoes can fit several [part|parts|After 'several', use a plural noun: parts.] of everyday life. A shopper may see a colour they like and imagine using the shoes beyond one [ocassion|occasion|Spelling: 'occasion' has double c and one s.].

title: The boy who cannot reach the shelf
text: In the advert, a boy stands on his toes to get a [bored|board|A 'board' is a flat piece of wood; 'bored' is a feeling.] game from a high shelf. His older sister moves it down to a low shelf, and they start playing. The low storage unit becomes [usefully|useful|After 'becomes', use an adjective: useful.] through the story. Parents may see how their children could [chose|choose|After 'could', use the base verb 'choose'; 'chose' is the past.] games without asking for help.

title: The letter from a customer
text: A toy shop’s poster shows part of a letter from a child who [recieved|received|Spelling: 'i before e, except after c': received.] a model plane. In the photo, the same plane [hang|hangs|'The same plane' is singular, so add -s: hangs.] above the child’s bed. The letter gives viewers a reason to believe the toy is still [enjoying|enjoyed|Use the passive: the toy is still enjoyed.] after opening day. A buyer may want a gift that [last|lasts|'A gift' is singular, so add -s: lasts.].

title: A table that opens for guests
text: Two people eat at a small table. When friends [arrives|arrive|'Friends' is plural, so use 'arrive'.], they pull out another part and make room for four. The advert waits until guests appear before [show|showing|After 'before', use the -ing form: showing.] how the table changes. This makes its extra space [feels|feel|After 'makes its extra space', use the base verb: feel.] like an answer to a real problem, especially for people living in small homes.

title: The café that gives cups back
text: A customer brings an empty cup to a café and [place|places|'A customer' is singular, so add -s: places.] it on the counter. The server takes the cup and gives a small [number|amount|Use 'amount' with uncountable nouns like 'money'.] of money back. The advert shows the whole exchange, so viewers understand how the return system works. Regular customers may like the chance to use [less|fewer|Use 'fewer' with plural nouns like 'cups'.] new cups and save a little money.

title: The slow walk to school
text: A shoe advert follows a child on the way to school. She stops to look at a beetle and then [run|runs|'She' takes -s: she runs.] to catch up with her brother. The shoes are in both shots, but the advert gives attention to the [childs|child’s|Use an apostrophe to show the morning belongs to the child: child’s.] morning. Parents may see them as shoes [making|made|Use the past participle: shoes (that are) made for.] for ordinary days, rather than special events.

title: The empty playground at dusk
text: A charity poster shows a playground just after the children have [went|gone|After 'have', use the past participle: gone.] home. The swings are still, and one light [remain|remains|'One light' is singular, so add -s: remains.] on. The words ask for help keeping the playground open. By showing an empty place that local families [knows|know|'Families' is plural, so use 'know'.], the poster encourages readers to think about what their area could lose.

title: The drink with a date
text: The date when the juice was made [appear|appears|The subject is 'the date' (singular), so add -s: appears.] on the front of the bottle. The advert shows a customer picking up two bottles and comparing those dates. This gives shoppers a simple way to [do|make|We say 'make a choice'.] a choice. People who like to know when their food was [preparing|prepared|Use the passive: the food was prepared.] may pay attention.

title: A map made from bread
text: Different kinds of bread [forms|form|The subject is 'kinds' (plural), so use 'form'.] the streets on a bakery poster. A small [role|roll|A 'roll' is bread; a 'role' is a part someone plays.] marks the shop’s place in the middle. The unusual map may make passers-by [looking|look|After 'make someone', use the base verb: look.] twice, but it also gives them directions. Someone who likes the picture can still find the bakery and buy the bread.

title: The boy reading the large sign
text: A child stands close to a museum sign and reads the words [allowed|aloud|'Aloud' means so people can hear; 'allowed' means permitted.]. The camera then pulls back to show that the letters [is|are|'The letters' is plural, so use 'are'.] large enough to read from a distance. The advert uses the child to show how [clearly|clear|After 'are', use the adjective: how clear the signs are.] the signs are. Families may feel more comfortable exploring without a guide.

title: The window that opens halfway
text: A woman opens a window while holding a [slept|sleeping|Use 'sleeping' for a baby who is asleep now.] baby. She stops it halfway with one hand and lets in some [airs|air|'Air' is uncountable: no -s.]. The advert shows the handle and the space for her hand clearly. Parents may notice how [few|little|Use 'little' with uncountable nouns like 'effort'.] effort the action takes when they are carrying a child.

title: A poster from the ground up
text: A camera starts at a child’s shoes and moves [slow|slowly|Use the adverb 'slowly' to describe how it moves.] up to the top of a climbing wall. We see how [highly|high|After 'looks', use the adjective: high.] the wall looks from below. The advert then shows an instructor standing [besides|beside|'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means 'as well as'.] the child. Parents can see both the challenge and the support available at the centre.

title: The music stops for a whisper
text: An advert for a hearing [aide|aid|An 'aid' is a device that helps; an 'aide' is an assistant.] begins with loud traffic and a busy café. The music stops when a little girl [whisper|whispers|'A little girl' is singular, so add -s: whispers.] something to her grandfather. We hear her words clearly. This change lets viewers focus [at|on|We say 'focus on' something.] a moment he wants to share. Older people may see a reason to ask about the product.

title: A bus ticket from a friend
text: A student hands a bus ticket to a friend who has never [use|used|After 'has', use the past participle: used.] the route. They get on together, and the friend [relax|relaxes|'The friend' is singular, so add -es: relaxes.] when she sees the stop near her home. The company uses their conversation to make a new service feel familiar. A first-time passenger may find the friend more [reassured|reassuring|Use 'reassuring' for what makes you feel calm.] [then|than|Use 'than' to compare.] a timetable.

title: The red line on the package
text: A red line [run|runs|'A red line' is singular, so add -s: runs.] across a packet of rice from the cooking time to a picture of the finished meal. This helps shoppers connect the instructions with the food they could make. Someone with little time for dinner may look at the minutes first and then decide [weather|whether|'Whether' introduces a choice; 'weather' is rain and sun.] the meal is worth [try|trying|After 'worth', use the -ing form: trying.].

title: An advert told by a neighbour
text: In the home repair advert, a neighbour describes the [broke|broken|Use the past participle 'broken' before a noun.] fence before the owner speaks. She has [saw|seen|After 'has', use the past participle: seen.] the problem from her own garden. This makes the need for a repair feel [really|real|After 'feel', use an adjective: real.] to someone outside the house. Viewers with a similar fence may think about what their neighbours can see.

title: The price on the last page
text: A holiday advert [spend|spends|'A holiday advert' is singular, so add -s: spends.] most of its space showing beaches and restaurants. The total price appears only after several pictures. This order encourages viewers to imagine the trip before [think|thinking|After 'before', use the -ing form: thinking.] about the cost. Some people may want to book by then, while others will still need to check what the price [include|includes|'The price' is singular, so add -s: includes.].

title: The single bulb in the window
text: A house in the poster has just one light on while the rest of the street [are|is|'The rest of the street' is singular, so use 'is'.] dark. The words ask people to use [fewer|less|Use 'less' with uncountable nouns like 'electricity'.] electricity in the evening. The lit window makes the idea [easily|easy|After 'makes the idea', use the adjective: easy.] to picture. A reader may think about which lights are still on at home.

title: The camera behind the goalkeeper
text: The sports camera advert places its camera behind a goalkeeper. When a shot [come|comes|'A shot' is singular, so add -s: comes.] towards her, the view moves with her hands as she saves it. The unusual position lets young players imagine [be|being|After 'imagine', use the -ing form: being.] in the match. They may want a camera to record their own [better|best|Use the superlative 'best' for the top moments of all.] moments.

title: The window made into a screen
text: The advert shows a family watching a film on a screen in their garden. When the film [end|ends|'The film' is singular, so add -s: ends.], they roll the screen away and see the window behind it. This change makes the [equipments|equipment|'Equipment' is uncountable: no -s.] look easy to [stored|store|After 'to', use the base verb: store.]. People with a small garden may imagine setting it up for one evening.

title: The timer before the school bell
text: A child [use|uses|'A child' is singular, so add -s: uses.] a small timer while packing a school bag. It rings just before she has to [leaving|leave|After 'has to', use the base verb: leave.], and she checks that her books are inside. The advert shows a use for the timer during a busy morning. Parents may imagine [less|fewer|Use 'fewer' with plural nouns like 'searches'.] last-minute searches around the house.

title: A question on the cinema ticket
text: The cinema puts ‘Who left the door open?’ on tickets for a new mystery film. The trailer [show|shows|'The trailer' is singular, so add -s: shows.] an open door but gives no answer. People may [carries|carry|After 'may', use the base verb: carry.] the question into the screening and look for clues. Printing it on the ticket [make|makes|'Printing it…' is one action, so use 'makes'.] even the small piece of paper part of the story.

title: A map with places to rest
text: A walking tour poster marks [benchs|benches|Add -es after -ch: benches.] and cafés along its route. The advert also shows a couple stopping [to|for|We say 'stop for' something: stopping for tea.] tea halfway through. This may change how people see the walk. Someone who likes exploring but worries about getting [tiring|tired|Use 'tired' for how you feel.] can see that they do not have to keep [move|moving|After 'keep', use the -ing form: moving.] all day.

title: A clock behind the teacher
text: A poster for an evening class shows a teacher at the front and a clock [read|reading|Use the -ing form: a clock (that is) reading seven.] seven behind her. The time is part of the picture, so viewers notice it while [imagine|imagining|After 'while', use the -ing form: imagining.] the lesson. Adults who work in the day can see that the class [start|starts|'The class' is singular, so add -s: starts.] after they finish.

title: The dress that changes with a belt
text: First, a woman wears a [plane|plain|'Plain' means simple; a 'plane' flies.] dress to work. She adds a bright belt before meeting friends that evening. The advert shows how one piece of [clothings|clothing|'Clothing' is uncountable: no -s.] can look [differently|different|After 'look', use an adjective: different.]. Shoppers who want to buy fewer outfits may like the idea of using the same dress in two places.

title: The warning at the swimming pool
text: A safety poster shows a wet floor beside the pool and a pair of [foots|feet|The plural of 'foot' is 'feet'.] moving slowly around it. The words ‘Walk, please’ [appears|appear|'The words' is plural, so use 'appear'.] at eye level. The picture shows why the request [matter|matters|'The request' is singular, so add -s: matters.]. Children who want to reach the water quickly may slow down when they see where someone could slip.

title: The cake made in front of you
text: Through a shop window, customers watch a baker [puts|put|After 'watch someone', use the base verb: put.] fruit on a cake. The poster says they can choose the fruit before the baker starts. Seeing the work and making a choice could make the cake feel [personally|personal|After 'feel', use an adjective: personal.]. Someone ordering for a birthday may enjoy [be|being|After 'enjoy', use the -ing form: being.] part of the process.

title: The weekend price beside the weekday price
text: A museum advert puts both ticket [price|prices|After 'both', use a plural noun: prices.] next to each other. The weekday price is lower, but the weekend price is still easy to see. This helps families [compares|compare|After 'helps families', use the base verb: compare.] days before they plan a trip. People with free time during the week may choose a [quiter|quieter|Spelling: 'quiet' becomes 'quieter'.], cheaper visit.

title: A message on the garden wall
text: The garden shop paints ‘Start here’ on a wall beside three small [pot|pots|After 'three', use a plural noun: pots.]. A video shows a new gardener [filled|filling|After 'shows a gardener', use the -ing form: filling.] one pot and adding seeds. The short lesson helps people [sees|see|After 'helps people', use the base verb: see.] what they need first. Someone who has never grown [nothing|anything|'Never' is already negative, so use 'anything'.] may feel able to begin with one pot.

title: The electric car without an engine note
text: At a red light, the driver lowers her window and hears a [conservation|conversation|A 'conversation' is a talk; 'conservation' means protecting nature.] on the pavement. The advert leaves the [voice's|voices|Plural nouns don't take an apostrophe: voices.] in the mix as the car pulls away. By letting an ordinary sound remain [audibly|audible|After 'remain', use an adjective: audible.], it gives viewers a way to judge how [quiet|quietly|Use the adverb 'quietly' to describe how the car moves.] the car moves. For buyers who associate a strong engine with a loud one, the scene also invites them to see quietness as a sign of progress.

title: Who gets the hero shot?
text: Finishing last [earn|earns|'Finishing last' is one action, so add -s: earns.] the most dramatic shot in this sports drink advert. The camera slows down as the runner crosses the line, and the music [raises|rises|'Rise' has no object; 'raise' needs one (raise the volume).] when her teammates come towards her. These choices give finishing the race the importance [usual|usually|Use the adverb 'usually' before 'given'.] given to winning it. The brand can appeal to viewers [whom|who|Use 'who' as the subject of a verb.] enjoy sport without seeing themselves as the fastest person on the team.

title: A room without a presenter
text: There is no voice telling us what to notice in the furniture advert. Instead, we hear a drawer [slides|slide|After 'hear something', use the base verb: slide.] shut and a chair scrape [soft|softly|Use the adverb 'softly' to describe how it scrapes.] across the floor. These sounds [turns|turn|'These sounds' is plural, so use 'turn'.] attention towards the materials and the way the furniture moves. A viewer watching on a phone may begin to imagine what it would be like to handle the [peaces|pieces|A 'piece' is an item; 'peace' means calm.] in a shop.

title: A running app that praises a slow day
text: ‘You showed up’ appears after a runner finishes a short route at a [gently|gentle|Use the adjective 'gentle' before a noun.] pace. The app could have [drew|drawn|After 'have', use the past participle: drawn.] attention to the slow time, but the advert keeps that number out of the shot. By praising effort, it gives beginners a measure of [successful|success|After 'of', use the noun: success.] they can reach straight away. This may make the app feel more welcoming to people who have given up [in|on|We say 'give up on' something.] exercise plans before.

title: An empty frame for the camera
text: On a camera poster, a blank rectangle sits [among|between|Use 'between' for two things.] two photographs of the same street. One shows the street at dawn and the other after dark. The words ‘Your turn’ [appears|appear|'The words' is plural, so use 'appear'.] inside the empty space. By leaving part of the poster unfinished, the brand invites photographers to imagine [add|adding|After 'imagine', use the -ing form: adding.] their own view. The camera becomes a tool for finding a picture that the advert has [leaved|left|The past participle of 'leave' is 'left'.] open.

title: The family photo behind the recipe
text: In an advert for a cooking kit, a teenager follows a [receipt|recipe|A 'recipe' tells you how to cook; a 'receipt' shows what you paid.] while an old family photograph stands on the shelf. The photograph makes a link between the new kit and the sort of cooking [past|passed|'Passed' is the verb here; 'past' means earlier.] down at home. It may reassure buyers who worry that using a kit will feel less [personnel|personal|'Personal' means private and individual; 'personnel' means staff.]. The ingredients [arrives|arrive|'The ingredients' is plural, so use 'arrive'.] in a box, but the meal can still feel like something they made for their family.

title: One wheel on the white line
text: In a tyre advert, the camera follows one wheel as it [past|passes|'Passes' is the verb here; 'past' is not a verb.] from dry road to standing water. There is no cut at the point [which|where|Use 'where' after a place or point.] the road surface changes. That [continual|continuous|'Continuous' means without a break; 'continual' means happening again and again.] shot makes the demonstration easier to follow because viewers can watch the same wheel through both conditions. For [cautiously|cautious|Use the adjective 'cautious' before a noun.] drivers, the visible change in the road may carry more weight than a general promise of good grip.

title: The poster that puts a pupil at eye level
text: In a poster for a [homeworks|homework|'Homework' is uncountable: no -s.] club, the camera is level with the pupil at her desk. We see the work [spreaded|spread|The past participle of 'spread' is 'spread'.] in front of her and the empty chair beside her, where a volunteer could sit. That angle makes the appeal [feels|feel|After 'makes the appeal', use the base verb: feel.] like an invitation to work alongside someone. Adults who worry they lack teaching experience may find this quiet scene easier to imagine joining.

title: The bakery that shows its mistakes
text: A bakery video leaves in the moment a baker drops a tray of rolls and laughs. Keeping that shot [change|changes|'Keeping that shot' is one action, so add -s: changes.] the tone of the advert. The baker seems like someone we could meet in the shop, and the finished rolls feel less like objects made for the camera. This can [built|build|After 'can', use the base verb: build.] trust with viewers [whose|who|'Who' is the subject; 'whose' shows possession.] prefer to know the people behind what they buy.

title: The missing finish on a desk
text: A desk advert places two close-ups side by side. On one, a scratch [reveal|reveals|'A scratch' is singular, so add -s: reveals.] a different colour beneath the surface. On the other, the wood looks the same all the way [thorough|through|'Through' means from one side to the other; 'thorough' means careful and complete.]. This comparison gives the customer a way to think about what happens after a desk leaves the shop. For someone who uses it daily, the marks it will show may matter more [then|than|Use 'than' to compare.] [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] appearance when new.

title: The bookshop advert with two languages
text: On a bookshop window, the same welcome appears in two languages in letters of [equally|equal|Use the adjective 'equal' before a noun.] size. The books beside it include novels and [childrens’|children’s|The possessive of 'children' is 'children’s'.] stories in both. Putting the languages on an equal footing [show|shows|'Putting the languages…' is one action, so add -s: shows.] that the second language is part of the shop’s everyday business. A family that reads in both languages may see the display as an invitation to browse [altogether|together|'Together' means with each other; 'altogether' means completely.].

title: The watch that belonged to someone else
text: ‘Previous owner’ appears beside a photograph of a small mark on a second-hand watch. The seller could [of|have|Write 'could have', not 'could of'.] cropped the image, but showing the mark makes its condition easier to [judgement|judge|After 'to', use the verb: judge.]. This choice also changes the way buyers might think about the mark itself. Someone who likes older objects may see it as part of the [watches|watch’s|Use an apostrophe to show the history belongs to the watch: watch’s.] history, provided the seller is [equal|equally|Use the adverb 'equally' before an adjective.] clear about how well it works.

title: The review with one complaint
text: A shoe shop places a customer review beside a product photo. The review praises the shoes for long walks but says they took a week to feel [comfortably|comfortable|After 'feel', use an adjective: comfortable.]. Keeping that detail makes the review sound more like an account of [really|real|Use the adjective 'real' before a noun.] use. A shopper might trust the praise more because the same customer has also [gave|given|After 'has', use the past participle: given.] them a reason to think [careful|carefully|Use the adverb 'carefully' to describe how they think.] about the purchase.

title: The date hidden by a peel-off label
text: A music festival poster invites people to [peal|peel|To 'peel' is to take off a skin or cover; a 'peal' is the sound of bells.] away a paper square to find the date underneath. Lifting the square [give|gives|'Lifting the square' is one action, so add -s: gives.] a passer-by something to do with their hands, which may make the date easier to remember. The design still carries a cost.
