Someone who is hurrying [passed|past|'Past' here means 'going by'; 'passed' is a verb.] may notice the unusual poster and leave without finding the main piece of [informations|information|'Information' is uncountable: no -s.].

title: An empty shelf in a games shop
text: The advert shows one empty space on a shelf and adds the words ‘Back on Friday’. This can make the game seem [popularly|popular|After 'seem', use an adjective: popular.] before the shop gives any sales figures. It also gives people a date to remember. The idea relies [in|on|We say 'rely on' something.] readers seeing the gap as a sign of demand, [despite|although|'Despite' is followed by a noun, not a clause: although an empty shelf could mean.] an empty shelf could also mean that the shop ordered very [little|few|Use 'few' with plural nouns like 'copies'.] copies.

title: A gardening advert set in winter
text: In a seed advert, a person [brushs|brushes|Add -es after -sh: brushes.] snow away from a garden step and sits down to [drawer|draw|'Draw' is the verb; a 'drawer' is part of a desk.] a plan for spring. We see the seed packets only when she marks out what will grow where. The scene gives the product a purpose before it is time to plant. It may reach people who miss working outdoors and would enjoy [have|having|After 'enjoy', use the -ing form: having.] something to look [foreword|forward|'Forward' means ahead; a 'foreword' is the opening part of a book.] to.

title: The pocket on the inside of the apron
text: A cooking advert hides the product’s [mane|main|'Main' means most important; a 'mane' is a horse's long hair.] feature until flour [spill|spills|'Flour' is uncountable, so add -s: spills.] across the worktop. The cook then takes a clean recipe card from an inside pocket. That small problem gives the feature a reason to appear at that point in the story. For home cooks who [covers|cover|'Home cooks' is plural, so use 'cover'.] their phones or recipe books in flour, it makes the pocket easier to [remind|remember|'Remember' happens in your own mind; 'remind' needs a person: remind someone.] than a list of features would.

title: A face hidden by the product
text: In the skincare advert, the model holds a bottle in front of part of her face. Viewers can see her smile but cannot study her skin [close|closely|Use the adverb 'closely' to describe how they study.]. The unusual framing [keep|keeps|'The framing' is singular, so add -s: keeps.] attention on the product and creates a playful mood. It also means that the image offers [few|little|Use 'little' with uncountable nouns like 'evidence'.] visual evidence for a claim about what the cream can do.

title: An empty bench in a crowded city
text: The park advert shows a [packing|packed|Use 'packed' (full of people).] street beside an empty bench under a tree. The two spaces [is|are|'The two spaces' is plural, so use 'are'.] only a short walk apart. This contrast makes the park feel like an escape people can reach during an ordinary day. Office workers nearby may value the short distance as [many|much|Use 'as much as' for how strongly they value something.] as the view.

title: The review beside the price
text: A customer’s comment appears [direct|directly|Use the adverb 'directly'.] below the cost of a camping stove. It says the stove was easy to use in strong wind but took longer than expected to heat water. Placing a mixed review beside the price [let|lets|'Placing a mixed review…' is one action, so add -s: lets.] shoppers [weight|weigh|'Weigh' is the verb; 'weight' is the noun.] a benefit against a drawback. The balance may make the praise more believable than an advert offering only [complements|compliments|A 'compliment' is praise; a 'complement' completes something.].

title: The museum poster with a borrowed voice
text: ‘I thought history was just dates’ is printed beside a photograph of a teenager holding an old [sailors|sailor’s|Use an apostrophe to show the letter belongs to the sailor: sailor’s.] letter. The words [suggests|suggest|'The words' is plural, so use 'suggest'.] that the visit changed her mind. Teenagers who expect the museum to be dull may listen to someone their age. The letter gives that change a cause, rather than leaving it as an [unsupporting|unsupported|Use 'unsupported' (without support).] claim.

title: A label that carries the story
text: On the front of a bag of coffee, a short sentence names the farmer who [growed|grew|The past of 'grow' is 'grew'.] it. The advert shows her checking plants before the beans are [packing|packed|Use the passive: the beans are packed.]. Connecting a person to the finished product may make it easier to remember. Buyers [interesting|interested|Use 'interested' for the person who has the interest.] in where food [come|comes|'Food' is uncountable, so add -s: comes.] from may look for the name again in the shop.

title: The lost glove on the train
text: A child leaves a glove on a train seat. Later, a staff member [find|finds|'A staff member' is singular, so add -s: finds.] it and places it in a [lose|lost|Use 'lost' (no longer found) before 'property'.] property box. The company uses a small object to show its care for passengers after the journey ends. Parents who have searched for missing things may recognise why this service matters, [despite|although|'Despite' is followed by a noun, not a clause.] the story does not promise that every [gloves|glove|After 'every', use a singular noun: glove.] will be found.

title: A food advert from inside the oven
text: The camera looks out through an oven door as someone places a tray of bread inside. Steam [brief|briefly|Use the adverb 'briefly' before a verb.] covers the glass before the door [open|opens|'The door' is singular, so add -s: opens.] again. This unusual view puts the audience close to the cooking [progress|process|A 'process' is a series of steps; 'progress' means moving forward.]. People who enjoy baking may pay attention to that detail, even though the advertised product is the oven rather than the bread.

title: An online shop that shows the queue
text: The checkout page tells customers that three people are looking at the same coat. This number may [makes|make|After 'may', use the base verb: make.] the coat seem popular and create pressure to buy quickly. Someone who [allready|already|Spelling: 'already' has one l.] likes it might complete the order sooner. The message gives no information about how [much|many|Use 'how many' with plural nouns like 'coats'.] coats are in stock, so readers cannot tell whether waiting would [actual|actually|Use the adverb 'actually'.] matter.

title: The restaurant with no food picture
text: The restaurant poster shows an empty table after a meal, with [using|used|Use 'used' (already eaten from) before 'plates'.] plates and a note saying ‘See you next week’. This [choose|choice|'Choice' is the noun; 'choose' is the verb.] asks viewers to imagine customers wanting to return. It may be more [memorably|memorable|After 'be', use the adjective: memorable.] than another close-up of food, although someone choosing lunch for the first time still has little idea what the restaurant [serve|serves|'The restaurant' is singular, so add -s: serves.].

title: A suitcase shown after landing
text: Most [luggages|luggage|'Luggage' is uncountable: no -s.] adverts follow a person packing. This one begins at an airport after a flight, when the case [roles|rolls|'Rolls' is the verb (moves on wheels); 'roles' are parts in a play.] across a crowded floor and lifts onto a train. Showing the end of the journey [give|gives|'Showing the end…' is one action, so add -s: gives.] the wheels and handle a reason to matter. Frequent travellers may judge a case by how it [behave|behaves|'It' takes -s: it behaves.] when they are tired.

title: The appeal that names a small goal
text: The charity poster asks [to|for|We say 'ask for' something.] the cost of one school lunch and shows a tray with an empty space for it. The small amount may feel [possibly|possible|After 'feel', use an adjective: possible.] for someone who cannot give more. By focusing [in|on|We say 'focus on' something.] a single meal, the appeal gives a large problem a clear first step, though the need will [continues|continue|After 'will', use the base verb: continue.] after that lunch.

title: The clock that refuses to hurry
text: A watch advert shows a family cooking while its clock moves [quiet|quietly|Use the adverb 'quietly' to describe how it moves.] in the corner of the screen. They take time to talk and finish the meal together. The watch is visible, but the scene gives it a [surprised|surprising|Use 'surprising' for what causes surprise.] message about time. It may appeal to people who want to use their hours [good|well|Use the adverb 'well': use their hours well.] rather than fill them.

title: The quiet customer in the busy shop
text: The camera follows a customer who stands silently while others [asks|ask|'Others' is plural, so use 'ask'.] for help. A shop worker notices her and comes over without [wait|waiting|After 'without', use the -ing form: waiting.] to be called. The advert presents service through a small action. People who dislike [ask|asking|After 'dislike', use the -ing form: asking.] questions in busy shops may see the [workers|worker’s|Use an apostrophe to show the attention belongs to the worker: worker’s.] attention as a reason to visit.

title: The bread that has to be shared
text: A large [loaves|loaf|After 'a', use the singular: a loaf.] takes up the centre of the bakery poster. Two hands reach towards it from opposite sides, and a knife rests nearby. The size and arrangement [suggests|suggest|Two things ('the size and arrangement') take 'suggest'.] that the bread [belong|belongs|'The bread' is singular, so add -s: belongs.] on a table with others. A person planning a meal with friends may think about bringing it home to share.

title: The market advert made of receipts
text: Old shopping receipts [forms|form|'Receipts' is plural, so use 'form'.] the background of a market poster. Over them, a large price lists what a basket of vegetables [cost|costs|The subject is 'a basket' (singular), so use 'costs'.] today. The design invites shoppers to compare the new price with what they have paid before. [It's|Its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] claim will only persuade them if the basket contains things they actually want to buy.

title: The warning inside a funny story
text: A road safety video follows a man searching everywhere for his car keys. The joke [end|ends|'The joke' is singular, so add -s: ends.] when he puts down his phone before driving. By making the audience [laughing|laugh|After 'make someone', use the base verb: laugh.] first, the advert may hold their attention long enough to deliver a [seriously|serious|Use the adjective 'serious' before a noun.] message. The final action gives drivers something [specifically|specific|Use the adjective 'specific' after 'something'.] to do.

title: The coat left on the train
text: A passenger gets off a train without her coat. The video follows a staff member finding it and taking it to lost property, then [cut|cuts|'The video' is singular, so add -s: cuts.] to the passenger collecting it. The service is shown through a small everyday mistake. For travellers who often have their hands full, knowing what [happen|happens|'What' takes a singular verb here: happens.] to lost things may make the company feel more [dependent|dependable|'Dependable' means you can trust it; 'dependent' means needing help.].

title: A photograph taken from the bus
text: A city tourism advert shows a famous square [threw|through|'Through' means from one side to the other; 'threw' is the past of 'throw'.] a bus window. The glass [catchs|catches|Add -es after -ch: catches.] a reflection of passengers, linking the landmark with the journey to it. The view suggests that visitors can see the city while travelling between places. Someone nervous about [find|finding|After 'about', use the -ing form: finding.] their way may value that sense of seeing the route.

title: A discount beside a school bell
text: The snack shop’s advert plays as the school bell [ring|rings|'The bell' is singular, so add -s: rings.] at the end of the day. A screen outside shows an offer for two drinks, and two friends stop to read it. The timing and the offer [works|work|Two things ('the timing and the offer') take 'work'.] together. Students who leave in [pears|pairs|A 'pair' is two of something; a 'pear' is a fruit.] may decide to share the cost on their way home.

title: The question on the mirror
text: ‘Who do you see?’ is [wrote|written|Use the past participle in the passive: is written.] on a mirror in a [photograph|photography|Use 'photography' (the activity) before 'studio'.] studio advert. Different customers stand in front of it, but the words remain in the same place. The question turns the studio visit [onto|into|We say 'turn something into something else'.] a chance to think about how they want to appear. It may appeal to people who want more than a standard portrait.

title: A garden poster with no green
text: The poster for a garden show is almost [entire|entirely|Use the adverb 'entirely' before an adjective.] brown. It shows soil, a pair of hands and small seeds just below the surface. By leaving flowers out, it focuses on the work that [come|comes|'The work' is singular, so add -s: comes.] before them. Gardeners may recognise that stage, while people hoping for a [colourfully|colourful|Use the adjective 'colourful' before a noun.] display may need the words to understand the event.

title: The café that sells a break
text: Even a short visit to the café [look|looks|The subject is 'a short visit' (singular), so add -s: looks.] like an escape from the working day. Outside the window, people pass in a blur, while a close-up shows a customer [slow|slowly|Use the adverb 'slowly' before a verb.] stirring her coffee. The two speeds make the café feel [seperate|separate|Spelling: 'separate' has 'par' in the middle.] from the rush on the street. For someone who spends the day watching the clock, a few minutes there may seem worth [pay|paying|After 'worth', use the -ing form: paying.] for.

title: A picture of the broken road
text: A local repair service shows a pothole in a street that residents [knows|know|'Residents' is plural, so use 'know'.]. The picture includes the corner shop beside it, so viewers can place the problem. The advert asks people to report other [damaging|damaged|Use 'damaged' (already broken).] roads. A familiar location may make the request feel [relevance|relevant|After 'feel', use the adjective: relevant.] to their neighbourhood and encourage them to look more [close|closely|Use the adverb 'closely' to describe how they look.] on their journeys.

title: The song sung by the customers
text: A local music shop advert shows three customers trying instruments at different times. Their sounds [overlaps|overlap|'Their sounds' is plural, so use 'overlap'.] until they form a [simply|simple|Use the adjective 'simple' before a noun.] tune. This edit creates a group that never actually plays together. It suggests the shop brings people into the same musical world, which may attract beginners [hoped|hoping|Use the -ing form: beginners (who are) hoping.] to meet others who [enjoys|enjoy|'Others' is plural, so use 'enjoy'.] music.

title: The white space around the shoe
text: Only one shoe [appear|appears|'Only one shoe' is singular, so add -s: appears.] on a wide, [most|almost|'Almost' means nearly; 'most' means the greatest part.] empty poster. The product name sits below it in small letters. The open space makes the [shoes|shoe’s|Use an apostrophe to show the shape belongs to the shoe: shoe’s.] unusual shape easy to study, even from across a station. Someone looking for a practical price or size, however, has to visit the shop or search online for more information.

title: The price shown after the game
text: A sports centre advert first shows children trying different activities. Only at the end does it reveal the price for a month of classes. The order lets parents [pictures|picture|After 'lets parents', use the base verb: picture.] what their children might enjoy before [consider|considering|After 'before', use the -ing form: considering.] the cost. Families with a [tightly|tight|Use the adjective 'tight' before a noun.] budget may still wish the price had [be|been|After 'had', use the past participle: been.] available earlier.

title: A shelf with two different labels
text: The supermarket advert compares [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] own product with a larger brand. It shows the price and weight of both [packet|packets|After 'both', use a plural noun: packets.] on the same shelf, giving shoppers a [fare|fair|'Fair' means just and equal; a 'fare' is the price of a journey.] starting point. A reader can calculate what each one [cost|costs|'Each one' is singular, so add -s: costs.] for the same amount. Taste is still an open question, so the picture cannot settle every part of the choice.

title: The coat size on the wall
text: In the shop video, a child stands against a height chart while a parent holds up a coat. The next shot shows the child moving [free|freely|Use the adverb 'freely' to describe how the child moves.] in the [chose|chosen|Use the past participle 'chosen' before a noun.] size. This makes choosing a fit part of the story. Parents shopping online may appreciate the [guidances|guidance|'Guidance' is uncountable: no -s.], though height alone cannot tell them how every [coats|coat|After 'every', use a singular noun: coat.] will feel.

title: A colour that marks each stop
text: On a bus route poster, each stop [have|has|'Each stop' is singular, so use 'has'.] a different colour. The same colours appear on signs at the real stops. A passenger can follow the [root|route|A 'route' is a way to travel; a 'root' is part of a plant.] on the map and then recognise the place to get off. The design is [especial|especially|Use the adverb 'especially' before an adjective.] useful for people who are new to the area and unsure of the street names.

title: A bottle with a marked line
text: The water bottle has a line showing how [many|much|Use 'how much' with uncountable nouns like water.] is left. The advert shows a walker checking it before [take|taking|After 'before', use the -ing form: taking.] a long path across open land. The line becomes a way to [do|make|We say 'make a decision'.] a decision, rather than a mark on the plastic. People preparing for a hike may see why knowing the amount [matter|matters|'The amount' is singular, so add -s: matters.].

title: A school advert that stays outside
text: The video never [enter|enters|'The video' is singular, so add -s: enters.] the classroom. Instead, it follows students leaving school, meeting friends and talking about what they learned that day. Showing their conversation [suggest|suggests|'Showing their conversation' is one action, so add -s: suggests.] the lessons continue to [matters|matter|After 'to', use the base verb: matter.] afterwards. Parents may value that impression, although they still need [informations|information|'Information' is uncountable: no -s.] about the teaching inside the building before choosing the school.

title: The last word on the poster
text: A poster for a reading course begins with a long sentence about a character walking home. Each line [remove|removes|'Each line' is singular, so add -s: removes.] a few words until only ‘home’ remains. This makes the act of choosing words part of the design. Readers may [wander|wonder|'Wonder' means ask yourself; 'wander' means walk without a plan.] how meaning changes when details [disappears|disappear|'Details' is plural, so use 'disappear'.], which connects the poster to the course itself.

title: The final shot stays on the viewer
text: A video for a photography club ends with a camera [pointed|pointing|Use the -ing form: a camera (that is) pointing.] towards the audience. The screen [become|becomes|'The screen' is singular, so add -s: becomes.] black before anyone takes the photograph. This open ending leaves the next picture for viewers to imagine. Someone who enjoys [take|taking|After 'enjoy', use the -ing form: taking.] photos may see an invitation to make something of [there|their|'Their' means 'belonging to them'.] own at the club.

title: The price of doing nothing
text: The home insulation advert opens with a family sitting comfortably in their kitchen, then overlays the [raising|rising|'Rise' (go up) has no object; 'raise' needs one.] cost of heating that room. Nothing [visually|visibly|'Visibly' means in a way that can be seen; 'visually' means relating to sight.] changes as the figures climb. This [restrain|restraint|'Restraint' is the noun; 'restrain' is the verb.] makes the loss feel more [credulous|credible|'Credible' means believable; 'credulous' means too ready to believe.] than a dramatic image of winter hardship. The campaign asks homeowners to see an ordinary evening as evidence of a problem they cannot observe directly.

title: The bottle beside an empty river
text: A drinks company places its refillable bottle on a dry riverbed, with the slogan ‘Every drop counts’. The setting [borrows|lends|'Lend' means give; 'borrow' means take.] urgency to the message, yet the advert offers no information about the water [using|used|Use the past participle: the water (that is) used.] to make the bottle. Viewers may respond to the image while still questioning the brand’s environmental claim. The picture is [emotional|emotionally|Use the adverb 'emotionally' before an adjective.] clear, but its relevance to the product needs [explain|explaining|After 'needs', use the -ing form: needs explaining.].

title: The invitation hidden in an apology
text: ‘Sorry we kept you waiting’ appears at the top of a restaurant poster. Below it, diners watch a chef [prepares|prepare|After 'watch someone', use the base verb: prepare.] their meal from the start. The [apparently|apparent|Use the adjective 'apparent' before a noun.] apology turns delay into evidence of care. It may persuade customers who value [fresh|freshly|Use the adverb 'freshly' before 'made'.] made food, though someone seeking a quick lunch could read the same [massage|message|A 'message' is information; a 'massage' is rubbing the body.] as a warning.

title: Two voices, one train journey
text: A commuter describes the train as time to catch up [in|on|We say 'catch up on' work.] work. Over the same footage, another passenger calls it an hour free from work. Neither voice [contradict|contradicts|After 'neither' with a singular noun, use a singular verb: contradicts.] what we see. By letting a shared journey support opposite desires, the company avoids [proscribing|prescribing|'Prescribe' means tell people what to do; 'proscribe' means forbid.] how passengers should use their time. The advert can appeal to both without claiming that travel feels [identically|identical|After 'feels', use an adjective: identical.] to everyone.

title: The poster that changes its pronoun
text: ‘We made this mess’ appears above a photograph of [litters|litter|'Litter' is uncountable: no -s.] on a beach. A second poster nearby says ‘We can clear it’. Repeating the pronoun [give|gives|'Repeating the pronoun' is one action, so add -s: gives.] the audience a place in both the problem and the response. That shared responsibility may encourage action, although it also risks [treat|treating|'Risk' is followed by the -ing form: treating.] people who did not leave the litter as [equal|equally|Use the adverb 'equally' before an adjective.] responsible.

title: One bicycle, two owners
text: A [scratching|scratched|Use the past participle 'scratched' (with scratches on it).] bicycle passes from a university student to a [youngest|younger|Use the comparative 'younger' when comparing two people.] neighbour. Neither owner replaces the marks, and the camera returns to them in the final shot. The second-hand marketplace presents [where|wear|'Wear' is damage from use; 'where' asks about place.] as evidence of a continuing life rather than [damages|damage|'Damages' means money paid after a court case; use 'damage' for harm.] to conceal. Buyers looking for a flawless product may resist that idea, while others may welcome the history.

title: The battery that survives the pause
text: Halfway through a video call, the speakers stop [talk|talking|After 'stop', use the -ing form here: stop talking.] while one person looks for a document. The laptop stays on, and a small battery [cymbal|symbol|A 'symbol' is a sign; a 'cymbal' is a musical instrument.] remains visible in the corner. The advert treats endurance as something that matters during an [unremarkably|unremarkable|Use the adjective 'unremarkable' before a noun.] delay. Professionals who have lost [works|work|'Work' here is uncountable: no -s.] to a dead battery may recognise the value of that quiet moment.

title: The bread advert that begins with waste
text: A baker gathers unsold [loafs|loaves|The plural of 'loaf' is 'loaves'.] at closing time and turns some into tomorrow’s lunch. Only then does the advert show the bread being [brought|bought|'Bought' comes from 'buy'; 'brought' comes from 'bring'.]. Starting at the end of a product’s day gives the bakery a reason to discuss [waist|waste|'Waste' is what is thrown away; your 'waist' is the middle of your body.]. The scene may earn trust from customers, provided they [understands|understand|'They' takes a verb with no -s: understand.] which food is reused and how.

title: A car advert built around a crossing
text: The car remains [stationery|stationary|'Stationary' means not moving; 'stationery' is paper and pens.] for most of the video while children cross the road in front of it. Its automatic warning system is visible, but the driver’s [patience|patient|Use the adjective 'patient' before a noun.] attention carries the scene. This places safety within human behaviour rather than presenting technology as a [completely|complete|Use the adjective 'complete' before a noun.] solution. Parents may value both, though the advert cannot show how the system [preforms|performs|Spelling: 'perform' starts with 'per'.] in every situation.

title: A classroom seen from the last row
text: The camera sits behind the [less|least|Use the superlative 'least' when comparing the whole group.] confident pupil during an advert for tutoring. We watch her hesitate, receive a quiet explanation and then [rise|raise|'Raise' takes an object (raise your hand); 'rise' does not.] her hand. Because the teacher is [rare|rarely|Use the adverb 'rarely' before 'seen'.] seen from the front, the scene keeps attention on the learner’s changing experience. Families may picture progress as participation rather than a [dramatically|dramatic|Use the adjective 'dramatic' before a noun.] jump in test scores.

title: An advert that repeats the wrong answer
text: A language app video shows a learner choosing the wrong word three times. On the [forth|fourth|'Fourth' means number four; 'forth' means forward.] attempt, she laughs and uses it [correct|correctly|Use the adverb 'correctly' to describe how she uses it.] in a conversation. Repetition turns failure into part of the learning process. Viewers who fear making mistakes may find this more [pervasive|persuasive|'Persuasive' means convincing; 'pervasive' means spreading everywhere.] than a claim that lessons are easy, because the difficulty remains [visibly|visible|After 'remains', use an adjective: visible.].

title: The price divided between friends
text: A holiday company shows the cost of a [rent|rented|Use the past participle 'rented' before a noun.] house per person rather than as one total. A photograph of six friends makes the division feel [naturally|natural|After 'feel', use an adjective: natural.]. This may help groups compare it with separate hotel rooms, but the attractive figure assumes every bed is [filed|filled|'Filled' means made full; 'filed' means put in a file.]. Anyone travelling with [less|fewer|Use 'fewer' with plural nouns like 'friends'.] friends would need to calculate the actual cost again.

title: The camera that records an absence
text: A family video advert shows an empty chair at a birthday meal. Later, the same chair appears filled during a call [projecting|projected|Use the past participle: a call (that is) projected.] onto the wall. The [devise|device|A 'device' is a machine; 'devise' is a verb meaning plan.] makes a distant relative present in one sense, while the first image preserves the fact that they are [physical|physically|Use the adverb 'physically' before an adjective.] absent. That tension may speak more [honest|honestly|Use the adverb 'honestly' to describe how it speaks.] to separated families than a promise that technology removes distance.

title: An ordinary voice over an extraordinary view
text: Wide shots of a mountain range [accompanies|accompany|The subject is 'wide shots' (plural), so use 'accompany'.] a voice describing lost socks, late trains and a difficult week. The contrast gives the holiday a purpose [grounding|grounded|Use the past participle: a purpose grounded in something.] in everyday irritation. Viewers do not have to imagine a life transformed by travel, only a short [brake|break|A 'break' is a rest; a 'brake' stops a vehicle.] from their own routines. The spectacular scenery feels more attainable because the speaker sounds [recognisable|recognisably|Use the adverb 'recognisably' before an adjective.] human.

title: The promise made by a closed door
text: A hotel corridor stays in view after a guest enters her room and shuts the door. We hear traffic outside, but none from within the room. The advert turns an [absent|absence|After 'an', use the noun: absence.] of sound into its [principle|principal|'Principal' means main; a 'principle' is a rule or belief.] evidence. Travellers seeking rest may find that persuasive, provided the contrast reflects a [typically|typical|Use the adjective 'typical' before a noun.] room rather than a carefully [chose|chosen|Use the past participle 'chosen'.] recording.

title: A bank advert built around a question
text: ‘What would you do with an unexpected £50?’ appears before any account details. Different people give [modestly|modest|Use the adjective 'modest' before a noun.] answers, from [replace|replacing|After 'from', use the -ing form: replacing.] a broken kettle to taking a friend to lunch. Their choices make saving [feels|feel|After 'make saving', use the base verb: feel.] connected to ordinary decisions. When the account finally appears, viewers have already considered what having a [few|little|Use 'a little' with uncountable nouns like 'money'.] extra money might mean to them.

title: The slogan written by the audience
text: A local library asks visitors to finish the sentence ‘This place is where I...’. Their responses [appears|appear|'Their responses' is plural, so use 'appear'.] in the windows, from ‘study’ to ‘see my neighbours’. The campaign lets users [describes|describe|After 'lets users', use the base verb: describe.] different kinds of value in their own words. It may be more persuasive to local decision-makers than a single [officious|official|'Official' means from an authority; 'officious' means too eager to give orders.] slogan, while still requiring evidence about who cannot [current|currently|Use the adverb 'currently' before a verb.] use the building.

title: The view from the delivery rider
text: A food delivery advert follows a rider through rain and traffic before showing a family opening their meal. The journey gives attention to work often [hid|hidden|Use the past participle 'hidden'.] behind an easy order button. It may make customers [appreciating|appreciate|After 'make customers', use the base verb: appreciate.] the service, but the warm [receipt|reception|A 'reception' is a welcome; a 'receipt' shows what you paid.] at the door does not [answers|answer|After 'does not', use the base verb: answer.] questions about the rider’s pay or working conditions.

title: The product placed after the joke
text: The video begins with two friends arguing over [whom|who|Use 'who' as the subject of a verb.] ate the last biscuit. Only after one finds it in his own pocket does the packet [appears|appear|After 'does', use the base verb: appear.]. Keeping the brand out of the opening lets the joke [works|work|After 'lets the joke', use the base verb: work.] as a small story. The packet may then be easier to remember because it [revolves|resolves|'Resolve' means settle; 'revolve' means turn around.] the disagreement rather than interrupting it.

title: The brand name spoken only once
text: Across several scenes, people mend a coat, refill a bottle and share a bicycle. The company name is [spoke|spoken|Use the past participle 'spoken' in the passive.] only in the last line. Delaying it [let|lets|'Delaying it' is one action, so add -s: lets.] the actions establish a [commonly|common|Use the adjective 'common' before a noun.] idea of reuse before attaching that idea to the brand. Viewers may remember the pattern of behaviour, though the company’s own role in enabling it remains [fewer|less|Use 'less' before an adjective.] clear.

title: The red mark that is never explained
text: A red circle appears in three posters for a new exhibition, each time around a [difference|different|Use the adjective 'different' before a noun.] everyday object. The final poster reveals that the objects belonged to people [which|who|Use 'who' for people.] lived on the same street. The [delaying|delayed|Use 'delayed' (given later) before 'explanation'.] explanation asks viewers to hold a question across several encounters. Someone who sees only the first poster may remember the circle without [know|knowing|After 'without', use the -ing form: knowing.] what to do next.

title: The child who interrupts the expert
text: In a science museum advert, an expert begins to explain a machine, but a child asks why one part [move|moves|'One part' is singular, so add -s: moves.] backwards. The explanation changes [coarse|course|'Course' is a direction; 'coarse' means rough.] to answer her question. This exchange presents learning as [responsible|responsive|'Responsive' means reacting to what happens; 'responsible' means in charge.] rather than scripted. Families may expect their own questions to be welcome, a stronger promise than [simple|simply|Use the adverb 'simply' before a verb.] describing the museum as educational.

title: The shoes at the end of a shift
text: A nurse [remove|removes|'A nurse' is singular, so add -s: removes.] her work shoes beside the front door after a long shift. The advert never shows the hospital, leaving her [tiring|tired|Use 'tired' for how she feels.] movements to convey the day. For workers [whom|who|Use 'who' as the subject of a verb.] stand for hours, comfort becomes the [inferred|implied|The story implies a benefit; viewers infer it.] benefit. The story’s empathy may attract them, although it supplies little evidence about the shoes’ support.

title: The phone camera behind the scene
text: Friends pose for a group [photography|photograph|A 'photograph' is a picture; 'photography' is the activity.], but the advert cuts to the person taking it, who is standing [lonely|alone|'Alone' means without others; 'lonely' means sad because you are alone.] in the rain. She then joins the group using the [cameras|camera’s|Use an apostrophe to show the timer belongs to the camera: camera’s.] timer. The feature solves a social problem rather than a technical one. Viewers who are often left outside photographs may recognise [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] value immediately.

title: The advert that refuses a perfect match
text: A dating app campaign shows two people enjoying a walk but disagreeing about the best route home. The final line promises an introduction, not [compatability|compatibility|Spelling: 'compatibility' ends in -ibility.] in every detail. This [modestly|modest|Use the adjective 'modest' before a noun.] claim may seem more [creditable|credible|'Credible' means believable; 'creditable' means deserving praise.] to adults with experience of relationships. It also gives the characters room to feel like people rather than examples of an algorithm’s [successful|success|After 'an algorithm’s', use the noun: success.].

title: The television reflected in a window
text: A family watches a nature programme while the screen’s reflection [cover|covers|'The reflection' is singular, so add -s: covers.] the dark glass behind them. When one child looks out, no birds are visible in their small garden. The advert then introduces a feeder. Linking the [distance|distant|Use the adjective 'distant' before a noun.] images on television with the empty space outside [give|gives|'Linking…' is one action, so add -s: gives.] the product a role, though no feeder can [garantee|guarantee|Spelling: 'guarantee' starts with 'gu'.] that birds will arrive.

title: The watch with an unreliable narrator
text: A runner insists she never checks the time, although the camera [repeated|repeatedly|Use the adverb 'repeatedly' before a verb.] catches her glancing [to|at|We say 'glance at' something.] the watch. The joke [gentle|gently|Use the adverb 'gently' before a verb.] exposes a habit many viewers may recognise. The product becomes part of her real behaviour rather than an ideal of [effortlessly|effortless|Use the adjective 'effortless' before a noun.] discipline. This self-aware approach could make the advert feel less like a lecture about fitness.

title: The silence after the sale
text: The assistant [hand|hands|'The assistant' is singular, so add -s: hands.] over a new bicycle, and the music stops as the customer rides away. We hear the wheels and the rider [breath|breathing|'Breathing' is the verb form; 'breath' is the noun.] rather than a final slogan. That quiet departure lets the experience [carries|carry|After 'lets the experience', use the base verb: carry.] the advert’s conclusion. It may appeal to cyclists who value the ride itself over the language brands [usual|usually|Use the adverb 'usually' before a verb.] attach to it.

title: The second photograph changes the first
text: A poster [initial|initially|Use the adverb 'initially' before a verb.] shows a man eating alone at a café table. [Besides|Beside|'Beside' means next to; 'besides' means 'as well as'.] it, a wider photograph reveals that his friends are just outside the frame, ordering food. The reveal exposes how much the first crop encouraged viewers to [imply|infer|Viewers infer (work something out); an image implies (suggests).]. An advert for a photography course uses that small correction to teach why framing [matter|matters|'Framing' is singular, so add -s: matters.].

title: An exhibition sold through one question
text: ‘Who gets called a hero?’ is the only line on a poster featuring a portrait with [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] face partly covered. The question suggests that the exhibition will examine how people are [reminded|remembered|'Remember' means keep in mind; 'remind' means make someone remember.]. Visitors interested in [historic|history|After 'interested in', use the noun 'history'; 'historic' means important in history.] may find that invitation more [engaged|engaging|Use 'engaging' for what holds your interest.] than a list of objects. Others may need a clearer description before deciding whether to buy a ticket.

title: The brand that admits its limits
text: A small line at the end of a bicycle advert says the helmet cannot prevent every injury. It follows a demonstration of how the helmet [absorb|absorbs|'The helmet' is singular, so add -s: absorbs.] a blow. The qualification [make|makes|'The qualification' is singular, so add -s: makes.] the safety claim narrower but [potential|potentially|Use the adverb 'potentially' before an adjective.] more trustworthy. Parents may appreciate being [gave|given|Use the past participle 'given' in the passive.] a reason to buy without being promised protection that no product can provide.

title: The empty supermarket at closing time
text: An advert for reduced-price food shows staff [placed|placing|After 'shows staff', use the -ing form: placing.] unsold items together after the last customers [leaves|leave|'Customers' is plural, so use 'leave'.]. The camera stays with the workers rather than following a bargain hunter. Their routine gives the offer a purpose beyond [save|saving|After 'beyond', use the -ing form: saving.] money. Shoppers may see buying the food as a way to prevent waste, though the products available will [very|vary|'Vary' means change; 'very' is an adverb.].

title: The film poster with the ending exposed
text: A poster for a mystery film shows its missing person standing safely beside the title. The real question becomes how she reached that point. By revealing an outcome, the campaign trades one kind of [suspence|suspense|Spelling: 'suspense' ends in -se.] for another. Viewers who dislike fearing for a [characters|character’s|Use an apostrophe to show the life belongs to the character: character’s.] life may be more willing to watch, while others may feel that [to|too|'Too' means more than enough.] much has been [gave|given|Use the past participle 'given' in the passive.] away.

title: A light that changes the evidence
text: The same room appears under a blue lamp and then under a warm one. In the first shot it feels [former|formal|'Formal' means serious and official; 'former' means earlier.], while in the second it seems welcoming. An advert for adjustable lighting lets viewers [sees|see|After 'lets viewers', use the base verb: see.] that mood is partly made by presentation. This is persuasive because the product [cause|causes|'The product' is singular, so add -s: causes.] the visible change, though furniture and camera settings stay [careful|carefully|Use the adverb 'carefully' before 'controlled'.] controlled.

title: A service explained by its least exciting moment
text: The parcel company [spend|spends|'The parcel company' is singular, so add -s: spends.] most of its advert showing someone changing an address after ordering. There is no dramatic delivery, just a [correcting|corrected|Use the past participle: a corrected label.] label and a confirmation message. Choosing this routine task [tell|tells|'Choosing this routine task' is one action, so add -s: tells.] viewers the service is flexible when plans change. That may matter more to [frequently|frequent|Use the adjective 'frequent' before a noun.] online shoppers than another shot of a smiling recipient.

title: The promise in a child's correction
text: An adult calls a community garden an empty lot. A child corrects him, naming the plants already growing there. The advert gives the child the [authorities|authority|'Authority' here means the right to decide: no -s.] to notice value others [has|have|'Others' is plural, so use 'have'.] missed. People deciding whether to support the garden may reconsider what the space [offer|offers|'The space' is singular, so add -s: offers.], even before the campaign describes [it's|its|'Its' (no apostrophe) means 'belonging to it'.] plans.

title: The cake that refuses to stay perfect
text: The bakery video shows icing falling [uneven|unevenly|Use the adverb 'unevenly' to describe how it falls.] onto a cake. Rather than cut to a flawless finished product, it leaves a small drip in place. The imperfection [give|gives|'The imperfection' is singular, so add -s: gives.] the cake a sense of being made by hand. Some customers may find that [appealed|appealing|Use 'appealing' (attractive).], while others will [expects|expect|After 'will', use the base verb: expect.] a cleaner finish for a special occasion.

title: The postcode beneath the photograph
text: A charity’s image shows a [damaging|damaged|Use 'damaged' (already broken).] playground, but the postcode below it [place|places|'The postcode' is singular, so add -s: places.] the scene only a short distance from the reader. That detail turns a [generally|general|Use the adjective 'general' before a noun.] appeal into a local one. Nearby residents may feel [enable|able|'Able' is an adjective; 'enable' is a verb.] to visit and see the problem themselves. The photograph still selects one view of the space, so its condition needs more than a single image to explain it.

title: The mountain printed on the packaging
text: A chocolate bar wrapper shows a mountain much larger than the small farm [naming|named|Use the past participle: a farm (that is) named.] on the back. The image may suggest purity and open space, although it says little about where the cocoa was [grew|grown|Use the past participle 'grown' in the passive.]. This gap [among|between|Use 'between' for two things.] atmosphere and information is common in packaging. A [carefully|careful|Use the adjective 'careful' before a noun.] buyer might enjoy the design while reading the smaller details separately.

title: A video cut before the applause
text: The musician finishes a piece, and the advert cuts to black before the audience reacts. A ticket link appears in the silence. Viewers must [decides|decide|After 'must', use the base verb: decide.] what they thought of the performance without being [guiding|guided|Use the past participle 'guided' in the passive.] by [applauses|applause|'Applause' is uncountable: no -s.]. The choice may respect their judgement, though it also removes the [socially|social|Use the adjective 'social' before a noun.] excitement that often helps sell a live event.

title: The word that makes a promise smaller
text: ‘Can help you save’ appears beside the price of a budgeting app. The word ‘can’ [limit|limits|'The word' is singular, so add -s: limits.] the claim, placing some responsibility on how a customer uses it. That modest wording may seem credible to people [weary|wary|'Wary' means careful about danger; 'weary' means tired.] of [financially|financial|Use the adjective 'financial' before a noun.] promises. It also means the advert offers a possibility rather than a result that every [users|user|After 'every', use a singular noun: user.] should expect.

title: The picnic shown from the dog's height
text: A camera close to the grass [follow|follows|'A camera' is singular, so add -s: follows.] a dog moving between blankets at a family picnic. From that view, a water bowl and shady place [seems|seem|Two things ('a bowl and a place') take 'seem'.] important. The advert for a pet-friendly park lets visitors [experiences|experience|After 'lets visitors', use the base verb: experience.] how the space serves an animal. Owners may appreciate the [detail’s|details|Plural nouns don't take an apostrophe: details.], even if they need a wider view to plan their own visit.

title: A caption that changes the photograph
text: The image shows a woman standing alone at a station. One caption [call|calls|'One caption' is singular, so add -s: calls.] her lost, while another says she is waiting [to|for|We say 'wait for' someone.] a friend. The advert for a news [literary|literacy|'Literacy' is the ability to read and understand; 'literary' means relating to literature.] course uses the same visual evidence to support two stories. It asks readers to notice how [easy|easily|Use the adverb 'easily' to describe how words direct.] words can direct their interpretation before they know the facts.

title: The farmer who reads the label
text: A farmer picks up a packet made with her [product|produce|'Produce' is food a farmer grows; a 'product' is something made to sell.] and reads its label aloud. She corrects a description that makes the work [sounds|sound|After 'makes the work', use the base verb: sound.] easier than it was. The advert keeps her correction in the final version. This gives her a voice within the product story and may make the company seem more willing to [listening|listen|After 'willing to', use the base verb: listen.] than a [perfect|perfectly|Use the adverb 'perfectly' before 'scripted'.] scripted testimonial would.

title: The luxury advert with a visible repair
text: A close-up of a handbag [reveal|reveals|'A close-up' is singular, so add -s: reveals.] a line of stitching where its handle has been [replacing|replaced|Use the passive: has been replaced.]. The brand presents the repair as evidence that the bag can be [keeped|kept|The past participle of 'keep' is 'kept'.] for years. Buyers may see durability in that mark. Others might question why an expensive product needed work, which makes the advert’s [carefully|careful|Use the adjective 'careful' before a noun.] explanation important.

title: The small number beneath the large one
text: ‘80% returned’ dominates a recycling poster, while the total number of containers [appear|appears|The subject is 'the total number' (singular), so use 'appears'.] in [smallest|smaller|Use the comparative 'smaller' to compare the two figures.] type below. The percentage makes the result [easily|easy|After 'makes the result', use the adjective: easy.] to grasp, but the second figure gives it scale. Readers who notice both can make a better judgement about the scheme. The design decides [witch|which|'Which' is a question word; a 'witch' is a magical person.] form of evidence most people will see first.

title: A building shown while being built
text: The housing advert includes unfinished stairs, exposed walls and workers still on [sight|site|A 'site' is a place; 'sight' is what you see.]. It asks buyers to imagine the future apartments from a space that is [visible|visibly|Use the adverb 'visibly' before an adjective.] incomplete. This may make the process [feels|feel|After 'make the process', use the base verb: feel.] transparent, but plans can change between construction and completion. [Perspective|Prospective|'Prospective' means likely in the future; a 'perspective' is a point of view.] residents need the final specifications as well as a persuasive vision.

title: The meal photographed before cooking
text: A food box advert displays raw ingredients arranged [exact|exactly|Use the adverb 'exactly' after 'arranged'.] as they [arrives|arrive|'They' takes a verb with no -s: arrive.]. A small inset shows the finished meal, but the larger image [ask|asks|'The larger image' is singular, so add -s: asks.] viewers to consider the work between the two. This may appeal to people who enjoy [cook|cooking|After 'enjoy', use the -ing form: cooking.] rather than simply eating. Those seeking maximum convenience could read the same arrangement as extra effort.

title: The voice that leaves room for doubt
text: A customer in a home security advert says the new lock helps her [feels|feel|After 'helps her', use the base verb: feel.] safer, then admits she still checks the door twice. The qualification makes her testimony sound [humane|human|'Human' means like a person; 'humane' means kind and gentle.] rather than absolute. Viewers may believe her sense of [improve|improvement|After 'of', use the noun: improvement.], while understanding that a product cannot erase every [worries|worry|After 'every', use a singular noun: worry.] about home.

title: The old logo under the new one
text: During a rebrand, the company peels its old sign from a shop window but leaves its outline [visibly|visible|After 'leaves its outline', use the adjective: visible.]. The new logo [fit|fits|'The new logo' is singular, so add -s: fits.] inside that familiar shape. This visual link suggests continuity while allowing the business to change its appearance. Long-time customers may feel [reassuring|reassured|Use 'reassured' for how you feel.], though the design alone cannot tell them whether the service they [values|value|'They' takes a verb with no -s: value.] will remain the same.
